reviewText: I bought this bag as a mobile professional, I wanted something that was both large in capacity not in size as well as very compartmentalized.  The bag's layout is nearly perfect, with only a few strange design decisions marring its utility.  For the price it was good but inside 2 weeks of use several components broke already.  That being said of products on the market this one is pretty unique, especially with the fold out back.  The key flaw that bothers me is the placement of all lift on the top of the flap.  I plan to correct at least the strap placement myself with the handle being of less concern.  I'll get into why its a major set back in cons below.The Good:Great material and general build quality, the layout of pouches etc is perfect and this bag is just extremely functional for any mobile professional weather a journeymen or a businessman.  The inside of the flap has a clear plastic sleeve great for placing a map or something else you would like to be able to view at leisure without handling it.  The back folds open to expose a great series of pouches for storing anything from small camera components to art supplies to tools.  The back aslo still functions with a separate flap as a quick access Velcro pouch for things you'll regularly need to get your hands on. The front, interior and sides are pretty typical bag layout with pouches and pen holders and a pocket perfectly sized for a note/address book.  You can fit up to a 16.5" laptop in this bag and still have room for a DSLR and some other toys/tools.The Bad:Cheap parts, the zipper pulls(the little string extensions not the zipper itself) are horrible, first thing I pulled one off with a gentle tug when opening a compartment.  Then the snap for the flap broke by the end of the week, note I only take my bag to work and back with me no back packing or anything intense it just broke when I was walking down some steps.  The shoulder strap is not of the same quality as the rest of the bag, while its made of the same material the stitching is not as neat, the clips don't swivel and the shoulder pad adds no comfort.  I would immediately replace this if I were going to travel with the bag.The snap breaking wouldn't be an issue if it wasn't so necessary.  The flap needs the snap because the strap and handle are secured to the flap.  This means that when you lift your bag you open it up to an extent.  The simple act of putting the shoulder strap so it lifts from the side would have alleviated many issues, as is you can't flip open the top and easily access the guts of the main reservoir with the bag hanging from your shoulder.  This is a HUGE mistake, and it seems like a rather stupid one with only 5 minutes of demoing the bag you'd have realized this limitation.  Shoulder bags are becoming more popular with fellas as they add function you can carry and access them more easily than a back pack etc, that is not the case here.Conclusion:This product is a series of trade offs.  To get a bag of this size with a similarly functional layout would typically be 4 times as much if you could even find its unique combination of features.  Sadly silly oversights are extremely damaging to this bags function.  A better strap attachment point would have simply removed the need for a flap fastener in the first place, lol.  Zipper pulls always tear away over time so that doesn't bother me too much.  However my brother was looking at getting the same bag different color as he loves the size/utility of it but I warned him away sighting my concerns and he agreed.  I'm a pretty pro-active consumer and will simply get strap clips stitched onto the side of the bag to resolve that major issue and keep on using it.  Being that it will hold the laptop I'm going to get and the camera I have plus attachments I'm a pretty happy guy at 35 dollars, still I don't understand why these cost free revisions weren't embraced as they would take this from a C product in need of light costumer modding to a AAA bargain.

reviewText: These rash guards DO run small, and are a bit short as far as arm and torso length (I'm 5'4", and about 128 pounds and the arm length isn't long enough for me) but the snug fit IS great if you are a competitive swimmer who needs a rash guard with NO drag and doesn't chafe in the process. These particular rash guards are really designed to be form-fitting to create less drag in the water for swimmers and athletes. They DO make rash guards with a lot more "room", and the way to tell is by looking at the product picture. If it hugs the torso in the product picture, it's designed to be skin tight like a bathing suit, not like a shirt. I hope that makes sense.I get a size SMALL in these (usually wear an 8-12 in clothes) and it fits just about right for me. It's comfortable, but tight enough that it creates very little drag when I swim. I swim in the hot Florida sun, two miles a day, 365 days a year, so I desperately needed something to help keep the sun off my skin.Because of the short arms and the fact that the rash guard will sometimes not cover the small of my back, I tried other brands (Dakine was the latest) to get a little more coverage. It was a mistake- I got horrible burns and irritations at the seams. Body Glove's products are built really well in that regard- even though I wear my rash guard skin tight, the seams NEVER irritate my skin.I'm not a total believer that the rash guard presents as much UV protection as it claims- I still get a pretty good tan when I wear mine every single day. But I think anything is a help.It's also nice and light, very easy to wash/rinse by hand and drip dry, and easy to tote around and pack. It's a nice soft material.It's not the best rash guard I've ever worn (I had one from Rip Curl that was a better fit, better at UV, but I can't find that particular model anymore :() but it's very high up there. I recommend it for swimmers needing some extra UV protection without chafing and drag.
summary: does run small, but if you are a swimmer, it's "true to size"

title: Suunto X-Lander Wrist-Top Computer Watch with Altimeter, Barometer, Compass, and Chronograph
description: The ultimate option for the outdoor enthusiast, the silver Suunto X-Lander wrist-top computer offers an accurate altimeter, a complete barometer, a precise electronic compass, and a multifunction sports watch in a single elegant package. Regardless of your excursion--whether it's climbing mountains, riding a muddy bike track, or skiing off piste--you need accurate, real-time information about your surroundings to pull off a successful trip. The X-Lander contributes by not only providing important data, but also keeping track of your activities so you can make rational decisions at key moments. In addition, the watch is user-friendly and solidly built, with a non-allergenic aluminum casing, a carbon-fiber back, a durable mineral crystal glass, and a water-resistant fabric strap.The built-in altimeter, which boasts a range of up to 29,500 feet, puts all 14 of the world's 8,000-plus-meter summits within the avid climber's range. Among the altimeter's functions are an altitude measurement function that lets you follow the vertical progress between stages, an automatic 24-hour memory that stores the altitude and ascent/decent rate for every hour, and an adjustable altitude alarm. Climbers will also dig the logbook function, which lets you record total and cumulative vertical ascents and descents as well as the number of runs skied.The X-Lander also displays the current barometric pressure and temperature--a must for activities in which weather plays a factor. The device automatically records barometric data for the previous four days, with the first six hours manifested in one-hour intervals and the rest in six-hour intervals. When the reference altitude is set correctly, the instrument also displays the present sea level pressure, which makes it easier to read and understand the barometric pressure at high altitudes.And few things are more important when exploring unfamiliar territory than a compass. The X-Lander's electronic compass contributes by guiding you with cardinal or half- cardinal points and a North-South arrow. The compass can also be set to track a certain bearing, which helps you follow a chosen direction. Meanwhile, the unit's declination adjustment function allows you to correct the difference between true North and magnetic North.In addition to the variety of outdoor functions, the X-Lander also displays normal time, with such add-ons as three daily alarms, a calendar programmed to the year 2089, a stopwatch with split-time measurement, and a countdown timer. Other features include a durable negative LCD display, a user-replaceable battery, and water-resistance to 100 feet. The X-Lander is backed by a two-year warranty on parts and labor.What's in the Box?X-Lander wrist-top computer, battery, user's manual.

title: Suunto X-Lander Wrist-Top Computer Watch with Altimeter, Barometer, Compass, and Chronograph
description: The ultimate option for the outdoor enthusiast, the silver Suunto X-Lander wrist-top computer offers an accurate altimeter, a complete barometer, a precise electronic compass, and a multifunction sports watch in a single elegant package. Regardless of your excursion--whether it's climbing mountains, riding a muddy bike track, or skiing off piste--you need accurate, real-time information about your surroundings to pull off a successful trip. The X-Lander contributes by not only providing important data, but also keeping track of your activities so you can make rational decisions at key moments. In addition, the watch is user-friendly and solidly built, with a non-allergenic aluminum casing, a carbon-fiber back, a durable mineral crystal glass, and a water-resistant fabric strap.The built-in altimeter, which boasts a range of up to 29,500 feet, puts all 14 of the world's 8,000-plus-meter summits within the avid climber's range. Among the altimeter's functions are an altitude measurement function that lets you follow the vertical progress between stages, an automatic 24-hour memory that stores the altitude and ascent/decent rate for every hour, and an adjustable altitude alarm. Climbers will also dig the logbook function, which lets you record total and cumulative vertical ascents and descents as well as the number of runs skied.The X-Lander also displays the current barometric pressure and temperature--a must for activities in which weather plays a factor. The device automatically records barometric data for the previous four days, with the first six hours manifested in one-hour intervals and the rest in six-hour intervals. When the reference altitude is set correctly, the instrument also displays the present sea level pressure, which makes it easier to read and understand the barometric pressure at high altitudes.And few things are more important when exploring unfamiliar territory than a compass. The X-Lander's electronic compass contributes by guiding you with cardinal or half- cardinal points and a North-South arrow. The compass can also be set to track a certain bearing, which helps you follow a chosen direction. Meanwhile, the unit's declination adjustment function allows you to correct the difference between true North and magnetic North.In addition to the variety of outdoor functions, the X-Lander also displays normal time, with such add-ons as three daily alarms, a calendar programmed to the year 2089, a stopwatch with split-time measurement, and a countdown timer. Other features include a durable negative LCD display, a user-replaceable battery, and water-resistance to 100 feet. The X-Lander is backed by a two-year warranty on parts and labor.What's in the Box?X-Lander wrist-top computer, battery, user's manual.

reviewText: My wife and I both have pairs of Beech Quatro yoga sandals that we wear only inside the house on weekends, when we're on our feet all day in the kitchen for ethnic cooking marathons. They really seem to be effective in reducing leg and back pain after long hours of standing. They're "inside shoes" only. We've never worn them out of the house, because we don't want to soil or scratch our tile floors with sand or stones picked up from outside. We had been meaning to get extra pairs for outside use for quite a while, but never got around to it. Then I found out about the new (as of Spring 2011) Beech Fusions, and decided to give them a try.The Fusions are quite a bit different from the Quatros, in appearance, construction, materials and fit. The soles of the two types are exactly the same size and profile, although the Fusions have a little more arch support (it's barely noticeable, though). The Fusions have a hard, textured rubber bottom rather than the softer, smoother material of the Quatros. The strap of the Quatros extends along the side of the foot like a conventional thong, while the Fusions have a wider crosswise vinyl strap like that on an athletic slide. This strap is softly padded on its inside surface and fits very snugly, unlike the Quatros strap, which is quite loose on the top and sides. The toe separators are the biggest difference. The Quatros' separators are made of elastic cords sheathed in black plastic tubing, which provide more separation than the Fusions' much thinner rolled-and-stitched vinyl thongs. They still provide the benefits of toe separation, but not as much. On the other hand, the Fusions are easier to walk in without the slight awkwardness of the Quatros.Bottom line: we're very happy with both the original Beech Quatro yoga sandals and the new Fusions. The Quatros remain for indoor use only, since our cooking marathons do not involve that much walking, which is less comfortable than in the Fusions because of the greater toe separation. The Fusions are easier to don and doff and easier to walk in, which makes them our sandals of choice for shopping, running errands and other trips away from the house. Regardless of which one you choose, you will realize at least some benefits in terms of posture, stamina and relief from leg and back pain. I didn't believe it at first (see my review of the original Beech Yoga Sandals), but now I do. They really work.
summary: Toe Separation in a Slide Sandal

title: Suunto X-Lander Wrist-Top Computer Watch with Altimeter, Barometer, Compass, and Chronograph
description: The ultimate option for the outdoor enthusiast, the silver Suunto X-Lander wrist-top computer offers an accurate altimeter, a complete barometer, a precise electronic compass, and a multifunction sports watch in a single elegant package. Regardless of your excursion--whether it's climbing mountains, riding a muddy bike track, or skiing off piste--you need accurate, real-time information about your surroundings to pull off a successful trip. The X-Lander contributes by not only providing important data, but also keeping track of your activities so you can make rational decisions at key moments. In addition, the watch is user-friendly and solidly built, with a non-allergenic aluminum casing, a carbon-fiber back, a durable mineral crystal glass, and a water-resistant fabric strap.The built-in altimeter, which boasts a range of up to 29,500 feet, puts all 14 of the world's 8,000-plus-meter summits within the avid climber's range. Among the altimeter's functions are an altitude measurement function that lets you follow the vertical progress between stages, an automatic 24-hour memory that stores the altitude and ascent/decent rate for every hour, and an adjustable altitude alarm. Climbers will also dig the logbook function, which lets you record total and cumulative vertical ascents and descents as well as the number of runs skied.The X-Lander also displays the current barometric pressure and temperature--a must for activities in which weather plays a factor. The device automatically records barometric data for the previous four days, with the first six hours manifested in one-hour intervals and the rest in six-hour intervals. When the reference altitude is set correctly, the instrument also displays the present sea level pressure, which makes it easier to read and understand the barometric pressure at high altitudes.And few things are more important when exploring unfamiliar territory than a compass. The X-Lander's electronic compass contributes by guiding you with cardinal or half- cardinal points and a North-South arrow. The compass can also be set to track a certain bearing, which helps you follow a chosen direction. Meanwhile, the unit's declination adjustment function allows you to correct the difference between true North and magnetic North.In addition to the variety of outdoor functions, the X-Lander also displays normal time, with such add-ons as three daily alarms, a calendar programmed to the year 2089, a stopwatch with split-time measurement, and a countdown timer. Other features include a durable negative LCD display, a user-replaceable battery, and water-resistance to 100 feet. The X-Lander is backed by a two-year warranty on parts and labor.What's in the Box?X-Lander wrist-top computer, battery, user's manual.

What can the Suunto Core do for you? For starters, it can sense an approaching squall even when the sky looks clear. This intelligent Storm Alarm--one of several intelligent features designed to keep you safe and secure--is activated by a rapid drop in air pressure over a three-hour period. Once the Core senses the change, the Storm Alarm sounds and flashes, letting you know that something unpleasant is fast approaching. The built-in altimeter, meanwhile, displays your current elevation, shows how much you've climbed or descended, and records your entire session for later analysis. Accurate to within 30,000 feet, the altimeter is an extremely valuable tool for mountaineering, backcountry skiing, and wilderness travel. Add in such features as a barometer, a digital thermometer, a weather trend indicator, and a digital compass and you have a terrific wrist-top computer for almost all your outdoor needs. Additional features include several traditional watch functions, including dual times, a date display, and an alarm; predicted times for sunrise and sunset to help you maximize your daylight hours; an automatic Alti/Baro mode that senses movement or lack thereof and switches between the altimeter and barometer accordingly; a depth meter that provides accurate water depth readings to 30 feet; and the ability to function in English, German, French, and Spanish. reviewText: I used to have a very expensive Marmot Exum Gore-tex shell Marmot Exum Jacket - Men's which I absolutely loved. Unfortunately I lost it and had to find a replacement. Although the Columbia Hot Shot II is not quite at the same level as the Marmot shell, it is a really nice waterproof shell and in different ways from the Marmot, has its own strengths.What I really like about the Columbia Hot Shot II is its extremely light weight. For camping or hiking it is fantastic since it packs so small. And the amazing thing is that once you ball it all up and stuff it into your pack, when you need it all you have to do is shake it out once and its essentially wrinkle-free and looks great. The sleeve length is good and the velcro straps at the wrist help you close things up in nasty weather.I also like that the jackets seams are all fully taped which assists in making it truly waterproof. There are also pulls for the hood and waste that aid in keeping the elements out.What I don't care for is at quick glance it seems like there are two inside mesh pockets. In fact they are the lining for the outside side pockets. Although you could theoretically use them as inside pockets, that's not their purpose. They also act as a means to provide additional ventilation to the shell... you un-zip the side pockets which then serve the purpose of vents in the jacket.The reflective stripes on the jacket could have  been more effective than they are but still they offer a minimal amout of night-time visibility and add a nice styling touch to the shell.There are no pit-zips in this shell.  I'm not knocking the shell for the lack of pit-zips, I only mention it. Under extremely strenuous hiking for instance, you can get a little warm in this and pit-zips would have been nice to assist in cooling/ventilation. But it's not a deal-breaker since you know beforehand that the shell lacks pit-zips so if you want them, just don't get this shell but choose another.My biggest gripe with the shell is that the attached, non-detachable hood does not have a stiffened visor. In hard rain, this is an extreme oversight since water literally streams down your face because the hood has no structure to prevent that from happening. Other Columbia products have a stiffened visor on their hood so this is an area that disappoints. A workaround for me is to wear a visored cap before pulling up the hood over the cap.Overall I'm quite happy with this shell for inclement weather. It is a good lightweight shell that is very packable and remains wrinkle-free. I like the Burnt Orange color for its great visibility and I'm happy with my purchase. I'm 6'2" and bought the XL size which provides good arm length and ample room for layering underneath.UPDATE: 12/1/2010 - I've been wearing this in some really rainy weather lately and I must say that the lack of stiffened visor is a real pain in the butt. I also feel that the jacket would benefit by being a bit longer in the body. I still like it for it's light weight and packability but it does have a few cons which I've mentioned.UPDATE: 12/13/2010 - I wore this as a shell the other day for some good hard XC Skiing. I had two layers underneath, a base layer of wool and a fleece vest. I was working up a pretty good sweat and this did not breathe very well at all. In fact, when I completed my ski and took off the shell, it was completely frosted inside. So I would not recommend this for hard exertion usage in cold weather.
summary: Extremely light weight and easily packable waterproof shell

reviewText: This watch and chest strap provides much information about your workout.  It is a stopwatch, interval timer,alarm clock, and heart rate monitor all in one.  The user's manual is detailed and easy to follow, which makes setting up your heart rate monitor to your specific preferences is simple.  You can also indicate your gender and weight and it will tell you the amount of calories you burned during your workout along with you minimum/maximum/average heart rate.  (I do not believe it is 100% accurate, but I appreciate having an estimate at least).  There is an option to have the watch chime whenever you are above or below your specified heart rate preferences, but I shut off this option.  Also, the heart rate monitor does not work unless you use the the chrono mode.  I almost always time my workouts, so this is not a problem for me.  Once you remove the chest strap (or it is 3 feet away from the watch), and leave the chrono mode, the data from your workout is erased so you might want to record it elsewhere if you are keeping track of this information.  The color, a bright pink, would not be my first choice, but it has definitely grown on me!  I have some concerns about keeping the chest strap smelling fresh as well, but that concern does not take away the value of this product.  I highly recommend it!

title: Marmot Women's Ama Dablam Jacket
description: The women's Marmot Ama Dablam is named after a Himalayan mountain, and is designed to keep you comfortably warm -- while traveling light -- in just such a setting. The durable down jacket offers maximum warmth with minimum weight, with enough urban style to transition to the city streets.FeaturesLightweight, super-warm down jacket100% polyester DWR ripstop main material100% polyester embossed WR lining800 fill goose down insulationAttached, adjustable down-filled hoodVertical front chest pocket for quick access to small essentialsInside zip stuff sack pocket allows you to stuff jacket into its own pocketElastic draw cord hem for adjustability in serious weatherZippered handwarmer pocketsAdjustable Velcro and elastic cuffs for comfort and adjustabilityAngel-Wing Movement allows full range of motion in arms without jacket riding up28.5-inch center back lengthMarmot DownMarmot often says that "down is in our DNA." The company was founded in 1974 as a manufacturer and seller of premium down jackets, vests, and sleeping bags, and continues to use fine quality goose down for its insulated outdoor products. Mountaineers and outdoor enthusiasts the world over rely on Marmot down gear for warmth, comfort, and sometimes survival.Down quality is determined by fill power and durability, which is dependent upon the age and maturity of the bird and the processing of the down. The best down comes from larger, more mature birds and goose down is generally better than duck down. More mature goose down has larger filament clusters than less mature goose down and these clusters, when grouped, provide many more trapped air pockets and therefore provide better insulation. To maximize the effectiveness of the down clusters, proper processing of the down -- sorting, washing, and drying -- is required to open them up.Higher fill power means higher loft, better insulation, lighter weight, and greater durability. Marmot tests all of its down for content, cleanliness, species, and fill power, guaranteeing minimum fill power for all down clothing and sleeping bags.Lifetime WarrantyMarmot products include a limited lifetime manufacturer's warranty against defects in materials and workmanship.About MarmotIn April 1971, University of California Santa Cruz students Eric Reynolds and Dave Huntley were in Alaska on the Juneau ice fields for a Glaciology school project. This was where the idea of Marmot, originally a collegiate climbing club, began. Reynolds and Huntley soon began making prototypes of down products such as vests and sleeping bags in their dorm room in Santa Cruz. By the spring of 1973, Reynolds and Huntley partnered with fellow climber Tom Boyce to open a modest rental and retail location, named Marmot Mountain Works, in a 100-year-old building in Grand Junction, Colorado.Their first large order was for 108, as the producer called them, "very puffy jackets" for the movie The Eiger Sanction, with Clint Eastwood, which helped make down outerwear fashionable. In 1976, Marmot was one of the first companies to recognize the value of a new technology being developed by W.L. Gore & Associates. Marmot was soon producing waterproof Gore-Tex sleeping bags, with Reynolds and Huntley testing early prototypes by sleeping in meat lockers and under fire sprinklers, and later introduced the waterproof/breathable fabric into nearly all Marmot products.From humble beginnings, Marmot and its product line have grown over the years, and today the company is headquartered in Rohnert Park, California, with offices all over the world and distribution in more than 60 countries.

reviewText: I purchase wallets frequently. Budget wallets, designer wallets, even leather specialty store wallets if they catch my interest. I find them interesting. I like to break them in, wear them out, switch them up. I'm a dork. Granted. However, I have NEVER owned a wallet with chain, or even just a plain old wallet chain rigged up with an existing wallet. So, I took the very affordable plunge that is this Carroll Tri-Fold wallet.The wallet is a tri-fold, as you will undoubtedly learn from the description above. And it is leather: Split leather, to be exact. So I cannot yet attest to the durability of this wallet over a long period of time. Split leather usually gives up quicker than a full on genuine leather, but the material they have mated this one with seems extremely thick and durable. So we will see (and for the price, how choosy can you be?). Anyway, to continue the features: there is a single, quite large, money pocket and two primary slots for cards and whatnot and a picture holder. A third, if you use together or remove the pictures insert. So if you are a heavy card user, this probably will not work for you. There is no "window" slot, for IDs or anything, so you will need to physically remove it when you are carded for anything that the young folks can't purchase. Also, there are two snaps on the inside of the wallet to hold it closed. Unfortunately, they are exposed on the inside of one of the card slots and I'm pretty sure they will bend whatever card is placed in that slot over time and with your weight. The stitching seems pretty good.Finally, there is a little rivet/metal lined eyelet that attaches to the chain, so that is good. The chain is not heavy, nor is it light. I have given it a good twist or two and a couple yanks and it seems sturdy. At approximately 12 inches in length, the chain is just right for most of us. The split leather snap for your front belt loop seems to be constructed of the same materials as the wallet body. Also, there is an extra little snap near the belt loop attachment for whatever you want, I suppose.Oh right, as with most tri-fold wallets this one is a bit fat. But... maybe a little fatter than your average tri-fold. So, consider that when you decide how much wallet bulge you want in life.For the price, it is a decent little set that I think will last a while. But watch out for the fatness, the snaps, and the lack of card slots, which may set you back.

title: Suunto X-Lander Wrist-Top Computer Watch with Altimeter, Barometer, Compass, and Chronograph
description: The ultimate option for the outdoor enthusiast, the silver Suunto X-Lander wrist-top computer offers an accurate altimeter, a complete barometer, a precise electronic compass, and a multifunction sports watch in a single elegant package. Regardless of your excursion--whether it's climbing mountains, riding a muddy bike track, or skiing off piste--you need accurate, real-time information about your surroundings to pull off a successful trip. The X-Lander contributes by not only providing important data, but also keeping track of your activities so you can make rational decisions at key moments. In addition, the watch is user-friendly and solidly built, with a non-allergenic aluminum casing, a carbon-fiber back, a durable mineral crystal glass, and a water-resistant fabric strap.The built-in altimeter, which boasts a range of up to 29,500 feet, puts all 14 of the world's 8,000-plus-meter summits within the avid climber's range. Among the altimeter's functions are an altitude measurement function that lets you follow the vertical progress between stages, an automatic 24-hour memory that stores the altitude and ascent/decent rate for every hour, and an adjustable altitude alarm. Climbers will also dig the logbook function, which lets you record total and cumulative vertical ascents and descents as well as the number of runs skied.The X-Lander also displays the current barometric pressure and temperature--a must for activities in which weather plays a factor. The device automatically records barometric data for the previous four days, with the first six hours manifested in one-hour intervals and the rest in six-hour intervals. When the reference altitude is set correctly, the instrument also displays the present sea level pressure, which makes it easier to read and understand the barometric pressure at high altitudes.And few things are more important when exploring unfamiliar territory than a compass. The X-Lander's electronic compass contributes by guiding you with cardinal or half- cardinal points and a North-South arrow. The compass can also be set to track a certain bearing, which helps you follow a chosen direction. Meanwhile, the unit's declination adjustment function allows you to correct the difference between true North and magnetic North.In addition to the variety of outdoor functions, the X-Lander also displays normal time, with such add-ons as three daily alarms, a calendar programmed to the year 2089, a stopwatch with split-time measurement, and a countdown timer. Other features include a durable negative LCD display, a user-replaceable battery, and water-resistance to 100 feet. The X-Lander is backed by a two-year warranty on parts and labor.What's in the Box?X-Lander wrist-top computer, battery, user's manual.

reviewText: As I am a cheapo who doesn't do enough diving to justify an expensive watch, I thought this watch could be useful as a basic rough depth and time indicator. As a watch it's fine, however if I wanted something that was just a watch I'd have bought just a watch, or if I wanted a watch that spewed out random numbers I'd just have bought a calculator watch and periodically mush buttons randomly .The first day I got the watch I decide to test it in my 1.7m deep pool. Bam, turns out my pool magically grew to 2.9m! And then shrank again on the second dive down 1.6. After that they were within .2m. I could live with that. Easily.The next inaccuracy was the day afterwards. Let's go for a freedive I said, it'll be fun I said, we can know roughly how deep we go I said.As soon as I entered the water and was making my way towards the site, the dive mode kicked in. The mode that's only supposed to turn on when you are below 1.5m of water. I was barely below the surface, in all seriousness the watch would have been, at a maximum, 30cm (1 foot for you imperialies) below the surface.So how do I know how far down I went I hear you ask? Literally no idea is my reply.On the next day of christmas, my dive watch gave to me a stuck-in button that was faulty. (Read to the tune of 12 days of christmas).As I'm not a complete cretin, and I like to get my moneys worth out of things, I always rinse off my gear in freshwater after going for a splash in the sea. This watch was no exception, I dunked it in a bowl of freshwater and pressed the buttons. Later that night, as I was dozing off, I checked my watch for the time. And it was blank. Turns out if you hold a button in for a while the screen turns off. This isn't super fantastic if the buttons are prone to sticking when accidentally pressed. Which they are on this watch.On the plus side I ordered if with Amazons express shipping and it came so much earlier than I was expecting. That's where the extra star comes from!So in conclusion. If you want an oversized time telling piece that also has the date, a stopwatch and a countdown timer that all work fine unless a button sticks, this is the watch for you. If you want to accurately measure how deep you've been and how long you've been under for, it is probably worth spending a bit more money. I've been trying to learn for so long that usually buying cheap means buying twice, but I love a bargin.ThanksAndrew MortimerEDIT!Wow, so I've now had this for 2 months, and, apparently, for the last 24 hours I've been under 3.3metres of water. Honestly, what the s***? Watch is clearly buggered and I'm about to begin the long, arduous and, most likely, unsatisfactory process of getting my money back. Damn you Pyle!

reviewText: I bought this shoe from my LBS because I read a review here about how the shoe size runs small, and I didn't want to mess around with the possibility of a mail order return. Here's my what I found. I take size 9 1/2 with Merells and Chacos, and a size 10 in Rockports. With these shoes size 10 fits perfectly. So I think the sizing is about right - at least for a medium-sized foot. Your mileage may vary.Something I learned from my LBS is these shoes can be resoled by Five Ten for a nominal charge. That's almost unheard of in this disposable world! Nice to know they offer this service. The shoes do seem very well-constructed so it may well be the soles could wear out before the rest of the shoe.I find these shoes very comfortable for pedaling. I think the ventilation is actually pretty good (I can feel air getting through the top of the shoe and cooling my foot) and so far I haven't managed to sweat these things out even on a fairly strenuous and long ride. I am more concerned about how warm they will be when the weather gets cold. Also, the sole is pretty stiff, which is what you want for bike riding. I think the sticky sole feature is dramatically overstated by most reviewers. I didn't have issues with shedding very much. It should be noted that the fur is a grey and white with some black highlights, its not slightly brown tinted like the photo seems. title: Casio PRW 3000 Watch
description: The Casio PRW 3000 Watch won't cook your dinner, carry your gear, or give you a foot rub after a long hike, but it'll do just about everything else you can imagine on your next trek, backpacking trip, sailing mission, or time-traveling adventure. This little aluminum, resin, and mineral glass case packs a mind-boggling array of tech tools, from an altimeter to a barometer to a compass to a thermometer, all run by a solar-powered battery that'll last for up to seven months on a single charge. The altimeter, which measures in precise one-meter increments, has automatic and manual logging functions and can hold up to 30 records of high/low altitudes, cumulative ascent and descent, with a range from -2,300 to over 32,000 feet. That's just the beginning. The PRW 3000 has a barometer as well, which has an automatic pressure-change indicator to alert you to sudden swings, along with a pressure tendency graph and pressure differential graphic to give you a longer-term idea of what the weather's doing. To keep you on course, the compass has a graphic 16-point display for one-glance orientation, a bearing memory to keep you on route, and declination adjustment so your bearing is accurate no matter where in the world you are. We haven't even mentioned the one thing the PRW 3000's designed to do first and foremost--tell the time. It receives six atomic signals a day to ensure you're always on time, has 12- and 24-hour displays and five alarms so you never miss a mealtime, and sunset/sunrise, time zone, and calendar data. There isn't even space to discuss the stopwatch, 100m waterproofing, automatic LED, power-save function, or battery-life indicator, but trust that they're there.

reviewText: First off - I hike fairly often, and have had MANY ABC watches. For the money, this watch doesn't come close to the Casio Pathfinder series watches. I have had my titanium pathfinder for a few years now, and this Suunto for about a month. I'm staying with the Casio.Pros: Looks nice, has many of the features you would look for in an ABC watch.Cons: Cheaply made bezel. The silicon or rubber band has given my wrist major "indian burn" / burned red marks on my wrist. This watch needs it's battery replaced, whereas the pathfinder is solar. This watch has already lost a couple of minutes of time, in the month I've had it, the pathfinder is atomic. It never ONE time has detected a change in barometric pressure - enough for the little weather trend arrow to bend. Yet, it is clear outside - then major rainstorm, despite having the exact altitude set on it. It is somewhat difficult to use, perhaps it just takes more getting used to.This watch is pretty cool looking and all, but, for that much money, it needs to be more useful and keep the time correctly. My wrist rash I have each time I wear it, may just be different from person to person. Who knows. Maybe I'll give the watch to someone as a gift. Too bad, it looked pretty sweet online.
title: Suunto Core Black Military
description: Building on the success of the venerable Suunto Vector, the Suunto Core keeps you informed of conditions while you hike, bike, or camp, making it a terrific companion for outdoor enthusiasts of all stripes. What can the Suunto Core do for you? For starters, it can sense an approaching squall even when the sky looks clear. This intelligent Storm Alarm--one of several intelligent features designed to keep you safe and secure--is activated by a rapid drop in air pressure over a three-hour period. Once the Core senses the change, the Storm Alarm sounds and flashes, letting you know that something unpleasant is fast approaching. The built-in altimeter, meanwhile, displays your current elevation, shows how much you've climbed or descended, and records your entire session for later analysis. Accurate to within 30,000 feet, the altimeter is an extremely valuable tool for mountaineering, backcountry skiing, and wilderness travel. Add in such features as a barometer, a digital thermometer, a weather trend indicator, and a digital compass and you have a terrific wrist-top computer for almost all your outdoor needs. Additional features include several traditional watch functions, including dual times, a date display, and an alarm; predicted times for sunrise and sunset to help you maximize your daylight hours; an automatic Alti/Baro mode that senses movement or lack thereof and switches between the altimeter and barometer accordingly; a depth meter that provides accurate water depth readings to 30 feet; and the ability to function in English, German, French, and Spanish. The Suunto Core carries a two-year warranty.

title: Suunto X-Lander Wrist-Top Computer Watch with Altimeter, Barometer, Compass, and Chronograph
description: The ultimate option for the outdoor enthusiast, the silver Suunto X-Lander wrist-top computer offers an accurate altimeter, a complete barometer, a precise electronic compass, and a multifunction sports watch in a single elegant package. Regardless of your excursion--whether it's climbing mountains, riding a muddy bike track, or skiing off piste--you need accurate, real-time information about your surroundings to pull off a successful trip. The X-Lander contributes by not only providing important data, but also keeping track of your activities so you can make rational decisions at key moments. In addition, the watch is user-friendly and solidly built, with a non-allergenic aluminum casing, a carbon-fiber back, a durable mineral crystal glass, and a water-resistant fabric strap.The built-in altimeter, which boasts a range of up to 29,500 feet, puts all 14 of the world's 8,000-plus-meter summits within the avid climber's range. Among the altimeter's functions are an altitude measurement function that lets you follow the vertical progress between stages, an automatic 24-hour memory that stores the altitude and ascent/decent rate for every hour, and an adjustable altitude alarm. Climbers will also dig the logbook function, which lets you record total and cumulative vertical ascents and descents as well as the number of runs skied.The X-Lander also displays the current barometric pressure and temperature--a must for activities in which weather plays a factor. The device automatically records barometric data for the previous four days, with the first six hours manifested in one-hour intervals and the rest in six-hour intervals. When the reference altitude is set correctly, the instrument also displays the present sea level pressure, which makes it easier to read and understand the barometric pressure at high altitudes.And few things are more important when exploring unfamiliar territory than a compass. The X-Lander's electronic compass contributes by guiding you with cardinal or half- cardinal points and a North-South arrow. The compass can also be set to track a certain bearing, which helps you follow a chosen direction. Meanwhile, the unit's declination adjustment function allows you to correct the difference between true North and magnetic North.In addition to the variety of outdoor functions, the X-Lander also displays normal time, with such add-ons as three daily alarms, a calendar programmed to the year 2089, a stopwatch with split-time measurement, and a countdown timer. Other features include a durable negative LCD display, a user-replaceable battery, and water-resistance to 100 feet. The X-Lander is backed by a two-year warranty on parts and labor.What's in the Box?X-Lander wrist-top computer, battery, user's manual.

title: Casio PRW 3000 Watch
description: The Casio PRW 3000 Watch won't cook your dinner, carry your gear, or give you a foot rub after a long hike, but it'll do just about everything else you can imagine on your next trek, backpacking trip, sailing mission, or time-traveling adventure. This little aluminum, resin, and mineral glass case packs a mind-boggling array of tech tools, from an altimeter to a barometer to a compass to a thermometer, all run by a solar-powered battery that'll last for up to seven months on a single charge. The altimeter, which measures in precise one-meter increments, has automatic and manual logging functions and can hold up to 30 records of high/low altitudes, cumulative ascent and descent, with a range from -2,300 to over 32,000 feet. That's just the beginning. The PRW 3000 has a barometer as well, which has an automatic pressure-change indicator to alert you to sudden swings, along with a pressure tendency graph and pressure differential graphic to give you a longer-term idea of what the weather's doing. To keep you on course, the compass has a graphic 16-point display for one-glance orientation, a bearing memory to keep you on route, and declination adjustment so your bearing is accurate no matter where in the world you are. We haven't even mentioned the one thing the PRW 3000's designed to do first and foremost--tell the time. It receives six atomic signals a day to ensure you're always on time, has 12- and 24-hour displays and five alarms so you never miss a mealtime, and sunset/sunrise, time zone, and calendar data. There isn't even space to discuss the stopwatch, 100m waterproofing, automatic LED, power-save function, or battery-life indicator, but trust that they're there.

reviewText: I've had my pebble for about 5 months now and I don't know how I lived without it. The most useful aspect of the Pebble watch is as a triage device for your messages and calls. Scenario: you texted something to your girlfriend 10 minutes ago. Now your phone is in your pocket and your phone alerts you to a new message. Is it your mom with some urgent family news? Is it your boss saying you need to call him immediately? So you set down your coffee, fumble in your pocket, pull out your phone and unlock it to find- it's a text from your girlfriend that says "lol".So what the Pebble does is let you know immediately what the text is, what your new email is, who is calling you etc. so that you know if it's something you need to deal with immediately or that warrants a response.I know what you're saying, "But taking your phone out of your pocket or purse only takes like 7 seconds..."  True, but how many text messages do you get a year? Thirty per day would be around ten thousand per year. How many emails do you get? What about tweets or Facebook messages? Reminder and calendar alerts? Multiply that times 7 seconds and you can see how useful Pebble really is.Also, the Pebble has vibration, so if you are in a meeting, or in class, you can simply glance at your wrist to read your messages, without the conspicuous rudeness of pulling out your phone and reading it while someone is speaking to you.Of course, Pebble also has apps that can do other stuff: control your music, find your phone, etc. With the upcoming version 2.0 firmware apps will be able to do way more. And of course there are the hundreds of cool watch faces to choose from so the look of your Pebble stays fresh.My one negative on the watch is that it isn't very scratch resistant. If you get a Pebble, you should really get a clear screen protector from places like GadgetWraps.

description: The ultimate option for the outdoor enthusiast, the silver Suunto X-Lander wrist-top computer offers an accurate altimeter, a complete barometer, a precise electronic compass, and a multifunction sports watch in a single elegant package. Regardless of your excursion--whether it's climbing mountains, riding a muddy bike track, or skiing off piste--you need accurate, real-time information about your surroundings to pull off a successful trip. The X-Lander contributes by not only providing important data, but also keeping track of your activities so you can make rational decisions at key moments. In addition, the watch is user-friendly and solidly built, with a non-allergenic aluminum casing, a carbon-fiber back, a durable mineral crystal glass, and a water-resistant fabric strap.The built-in altimeter, which boasts a range of up to 29,500 feet, puts all 14 of the world's 8,000-plus-meter summits within the avid climber's range. Among the altimeter's functions are an altitude measurement function that lets you follow the vertical progress between stages, an automatic 24-hour memory that stores the altitude and ascent/decent rate for every hour, and an adjustable altitude alarm. Climbers will also dig the logbook function, which lets you record total and cumulative vertical ascents and descents as well as the number of runs skied.The X-Lander also displays the current barometric pressure and temperature--a must for activities in which weather plays a factor. The device automatically records barometric data for the previous four days, with the first six hours manifested in one-hour intervals and the rest in six-hour intervals. When the reference altitude is set correctly, the instrument also displays the present sea level pressure, which makes it easier to read and understand the barometric pressure at high altitudes.And few things are more important when exploring unfamiliar territory than a compass. The compass can also be set to track a certain bearing, which helps you follow a chosen direction. Meanwhile, the unit's declination adjustment function allows you to correct the difference between true North and magnetic North.In addition to the variety of outdoor functions, the X-Lander also displays normal time, with such add-ons as three daily alarms, a calendar programmed to the year 2089, a stopwatch with split-time measurement, and a countdown timer. reviewText: I bought this watch on sale at a department store and thought I got a deal...until I searched Amazon and found it cheaper here by about $5. Anyway, the altimeter is within 100 feet out of the box. In Michigan, it reads 600 ft to 800 ft on my one hour commute from home to work. I looked up the elevation of the two cities and this is within 100 ft.I am at the beach in Florida as I write this and it reads - 40 feet at actual sea level. This is accurate enough for me. Through the mountains on the way here, it varied from 200 feet to 1800 feet. I bought it to take with me on my trip to Machu Picchu.The barometer is also accurate, once calibrated, and changes in pressure can be used to predict changes in weather. In the US, in range of a network, you can get ten day forecasts hour to hour on your smart phone, but out in the "bush" it may help. I like having the world tie function and the stopwatch and countdown timers. I have used the alarm mode also and find it loud enough to wake me up, barely.The thermometer is a bit of a disappointment as you have to take the watch off and let it sit for quite a while to get the temp. This will let me know the temp when I wake up camping, if I took it off at night, but on the move, it reads your skin temp. I wonder why they don't put the temp sensor on the top of the watch far from your skin? It does tell me the water temp when I swim and has fairly good accuracy in water. I was in a hot tub and it read 106 degrees.Overall, for about $50, this is a great watch. I did not buy the Pathfinder types starting at about $140 here as they are too big. This watch is plenty big, but it is very light and does not bother me on my wrist. Those Pathfinder models look huge in the customer pictures and seem better for men with really big arms/wrists. I am 6'4" and weigh about 190, so I am on the thin side. Being a triathlete and swimmer, I need a watch I can wear in the pool, while running, and on my bike, so it can't be some big clunky thing.

reviewText: UPDATE May 20, 2014.  After testing the new firmware update for a few weeks I believe previous pairing issues between my pebble and Mapmyfitness have been solved.  The firmware update was described as addressing connectivity issues with certain fitness apps.  Apparently so.  Therefore, I am upgrading my rating and, feeling generous, I will give it five stars despite the teething issues.  It now does everything I expected of it without hiccups.ORIGINAL REVIEW:  Bought this at a local retailer as I was in a hurry.  So this is not a verified Amazon purchase.  I really want to love and use my red pebble watch.  It looks cool and simplifies my workout experience so much when it works.Therein lies the problem.  It doesn't always pair properly. I am using the Mapmyfitness app on an LG Optimus Pro G cell phone.  Not dated technology.  The watch shows paired to the phone via bluetooth, the phone shows paired to the watch, but it isn't always so.  Sometimes it works fine. Then, sometimes during mid workout, the connection stops - even though it still shows as paired.  I log onto the getpebble.com site and follow their instructions carefully - unpairing, turning both devices off, etc - and they show paired but there is still no connection.Of course sometimes it does pair properly and stay that way for days.Perhaps pairing is better with the iphone?  I don't know but I do know this is very frustrating and I have spent far too much time fooling around with pairing and trying to get the watch to work properly in this regard.I am not super technical but I am not a moron.  I've slaved new drives into my PC, upgraded cards, fans and power supplies etc. so I can follow instructions, am not intimidated by technology, and think I am doing everything correctly to make this work.  Could it be my phone?  I guess so.  Could it be the mapmyfitness software?  I doubt it.  That seems to keep working fine and is certified to be pebble compatible.I really cannot recommend this device given the problems I am having with it. But, because it could be my phone I am giving three stars instead of the two I think it deserves.

reviewText: Chose this to replace a 10 year old model with identical features - the old band finally packed it in and a hole had actually worn in one of the buttons (the adjust button); so I can say it gave very good service despite a real flogging over the years; and it still works perfectly. There are enough buttons to quickly scroll to each function and set easily without tedious menu scrolling.  You should find the stopwatch function par excellence with easy start/stop/lap selection via the front buttons.  I use this a lot for swimming laps; using it for running etc is an absolute cinch.  The manual does say not to operate the buttons underwater; I did with the old one at shallow depths (i.e. lap swimming) with no problems.This watch does the job brilliantly and is superb value. I'll get back to you in 10 years re the battery life, but if it goes close that long, I'll give it the full 5 stars!

reviewText: I decided to try these for my casual summer dresses and for a formal strapless dress I wore to a wedding. The instructions are easy to follow, and the lift they provide is excellent if you want a natural, bra-less look as opposed to a push-up look (I'm a C cup, about 36). They do look a little funny in the nude, as they cause a pucker or fold in the skin, but once you're dressed, no one would ever guess your little trick. ;) And they stayed on in sweaty conditions, dancing, etc. I decided to REALLY test them by keeping them on overnight and then wearing them in a rugby game the next day, under two sports bras. They actually stayed almost totally in place through the 80-minute game.There may be issues with some low-cut dresses where the adhesive might show -- I solved this problem by using fashion tape to secure my dress just above where the adhesive was. I have a casual knit dress with a plunging V that I've worn these with, and they didn't show, but again I secured the dress with fashion tape to avoid any potential accidental exposure. :)I didn't experience pain from the lifting or the adhesive like some other commenters have. My only note of caution (echoing the instructions that come with the product) is to take them off VERY slowly because I made the mistake of removing them in a hurry the first time, and I did suffer some blistering and raw skin, and maybe a bit of skin torn off. The next time, I removed them VERY slowly and it was fine. (I had been sweating so the moisture probably helped.) There was a bit of blotchy reddening in some spots, but it faded quickly.On a side note, I've been thrilled with all of the Hollywood Fashion Tape products I've tried -- the tape strips and multi-pack of different size tapes for clothing. I've ordered all of them through Amazon and they've all arrived quickly. Highly recommend!

reviewText: My first watch was a little blue and green affair that looked like a lily, and when you pressed a button, the lily flipped up and a little frog sprang out on a spring. Then aged 11, I got a Casio F91W and have never looked back. The strap breaks for me, on average, every three years (I wear it tight and the plastic strap gets bent 180 degrees regularly), but besides that I've never had a problem.I thought briefly this year about getting a smart watch, but the fact is, you simply don't need a watch to do anything else than the Casio does. It tells you the time, lets you time things, and sets alarm to remind you of the time. It has one brief, and it sticks to it. And it does it forever, without complaints, without worries about it being stolen, and without ever running out of battery. I keep all my old watches, so my room is like a graveyard of Casio F91Ws, and not *one* of them has run out of battery - the only reason I'm having to get another one is because it's so cheap, it's easier to buy one than have it repaired. More money for Casio, I figure.If you want to carry around a piece of expensive digital technology with the time on it that will regularly fail on you because you haven't charged it in 12 hours, get an iPhone. If you want a watch that tells you the time, there's an entire community of Casio buddies all over the world waiting to notice your watch and "Hey, you've got the Casio too! Aren't they cool?!" - and then say nothing else because the Casio is so Spartan, so obvious, so reliable in its simplicity the only real question you ask is "Do you have the backlight?"Long live the Casio F91W!

reviewText: I had wanted a pair of these shoes for quite awhile but the price was way out of my budget.  I was thrilled to find them on sale online a few weeks ago and promptly ordered a pair.  I normally wear a size 8.5 in women's shoes, but accidentally ordered a 9.  Turns out that it's OK to have 1/2 size bigger, at least for now.  I wear them both with and without socks.I suffer from kidney disease which is causing my abdomen to swell slowly and therefore brings strain on my lower back muscles.  After only a week of wearing these shoes, I literally have no lower back pain.  I don't know what it is about them, but they sort of force you to stand up straight and tuck your stomach in, but not in an obvious way, you don't even realize you're doing it.The second thing is, my feet have very low arches, standing for a long time was causing not only my lower back to ache, but my feet would cramp terribly.  Now I can walk/stand for as long as I like without anything other than normal fatigue.They look a little goofy if you're sitting, because the heels are so thick.  But when you're standing, they look like any other shoe.The positive side to all of this is that I like wearing them so much that I'm much more active, it's fun to walk around because it's almost like gliding.  I haven't tried the slow running yet, but plan to eventually (once I find a good sports bra).  The biggest adjustment I had to them is going down stairs, your balance is different so it takes a little getting used to.I had no "breaking in" time at all with them, I put them on the day after I got them and wear them all day long with only good results.
summary: LOVE 'em, everything they say they are and better

reviewText: I bought this watch to replace a 16-year old ironman triathlon which kept time very precisely, had a remarkably long battery life, and survived thick and thin.  I dropped it countless times, and even put it through the laundry once when I forgot it in my pocket.  It kept working, even though one of the screws securing the back plate was missing!  The last time I dropped it the battery was dislodged.  Once I slid the battery back it started working again, but I seemed to have erred in the reassembly because the two front buttons don't work now, which means I can't *set* the watch without disassembling it.  It probably would have lasted another 16 years if I hadn't been more careful while trying to service it.I am hoping the new watch will last at least as long as the old one.== PROS ==1. One difference between this and the old watch that I really like is that setting the watch is much easier, as noted by other reviewers.  When setting the watch, additional display elements appear which literally guide you through the process.  Also the ability to go backwards is especially nice, although I recall my older one let me set the tens digit and the ones digit of the minutes separately, which IMO is at least as good.2. You can set two different times on this watch and switch between them.  The maker calls this a 'second time zone,' although in truth you can set a completely different date as well, which in my case turns out to be very useful.3. The display is very legible.  The LCD contrast is noticeably higher than on my old watch.== INTERESTING ==1. The indiglo feature, when viewed in low-light conditions, is light-on-black.  It may be slightly more legible in the dark than the old watch, but in normal lighting it makes the display more difficult to read.2. The indiglo lights up automatically when the alarm sounds, making it possible to read the display in the dark without even pushing a button (apparently timex engineers think people use the watch as an alarm clock, see more below), but as already noted more difficult to read in normal light.3. There are weekday only/weekend only alarm options.4. You can choose between MM-DD and DD.MM displays5. The loose end of the strap clicks in very securely to the sliding loop.  It's very snug and getting it in is a little more work than I'm used to, but it's nice to know that it won't be slipping around, which is a problem I've had with other watch bands.  (I replaced the band for a different reason, noted below.)== CONS ==1. Size.  This watch is a monster compared to my old one, and I hesitated before ordering it on account of the size.  It is at least 30% wider, almost twice as thick, and quite a bit heavier!  I don't understand why anyone would want a watch so large and heavy.2. The band is molded into a form which curves down around the top of the wrist, so it isn't possible to take the watch off and lay it down flat on a table.  That's a common use case for me.  Fortunately, I was able to have a different band put on it.3. Start/stop are two different buttons.  This makes using the timer and chronograph features more awkward with this watch than the old one, and I end up fumbling to find the right button to stop it.  Not useful at all for timing very short intervals.4. Automatic 'snooze' alarm.  If you don't push a button to stop the alarm *while it is beeping*, it will beep again after five minutes.  If you let the watch beep for the full 20 seconds, then the only way to prevent it from beeping again is to turn off the alarm.  I consider this an annoyance.  I don't always have a hand free to push a button on the watch, and I don't appreciate the fact that it's going to beep again.  Snooze might make sense on an alarm clock, but IMO not on a wrist watch.5. It's difficult to turn the 'chime' feature on/off.  Apparently this can only be done while going through the sequence of actually setting the time.  On the old watch, turning the chime and the alarm off and on was done with a single button while in 'alarm' mode.6. The old watch would show the current time in the top half of the display while setting the alarm.  This was a particularly handy feature which always impressed me.  The new watch doesn't do that.7. When setting the time, timer, and alarm, there is a noticeable delay during which the next, done, +, - indicators flash but it is not possible to actually do anything.  I find this somewhat annoying.To sum, I'm glad the ironman triathalon watches are still around.  I'm happy with this watch.  Nonetheless, I liked the older model better.  IMO this is another example of the adage 'newer is not necessarily better.'

reviewText: Like: takes AA batteries so I don't have to use a power outlet, good battery life, display numbers very readable. Really like having sunrise and sunset times, that's extremely helpful. Option to display hunting vs fishing data at the touch of a button.Not so much: remote (outdoor) sensor frequently becomes un-synced from base station, esp. during colder weather despite fresh batteries. Have to unscrew the back of the remote sensor to change batteries and push the reset button and this is fussy. Remote sensor sometimes seems to report inaccurate temps but maybe that's because it's close to the house. A little tricky to set the tide station and other settings; for the love of god don't lose the instruction sheet as this is not intuitive. The # of tide stations available is a bit limited; serious fishermen may need a more expensive unit. Labels for the display numbers are tiny but not much of a problem once you get to know where each number is.Its not a watch as the title says, its a weather station. Have not yet checked the tide diagram accuracy against actual conditions or tried any of the alarm functions.

reviewText: This watch is amazing. It predicts the future! The watch can predict if my joints are going to hurt while looking nice on my wrist. Before I got this watch I did not know what low and high atmospheric pressure meant. Yes I heard it thousand of times on TV but I had no idea that the atmospheric pressure was so important and that is had to do so much with the weather patterns. The only thing I knew is that when the weather was bad my joints would hurt. Now I know why.The compass feature works. It will show me the right way and works perfectly. The altimeter feature is awesome, it will tell me when I will run out air and will get very tired easily. I is almost like a crystal ball that foresees the future.The sunrise sunset time feature is great. It tells me how many hours of sunlight in a particular day of the year I will have. Nice feature if you do not want to be stuck in the dark. Please note that the default sunset and sunrise calculation is Japan. You will have to read the manual to find your place in the world and set the watch correctly.The world time feature will show you where in the world is 5 pm so you get out of work.The titanium band will ensure I do not have to worry about it for several years. My other plastic and metal solar watches bands always go bad before the watch does. I own several solar watches with broken plastic and metal bands. Just one word of advice, if you are removing the links your self to resize the band, be very careful with a little spacer that holds the pin inside the link. If you loose that, the pin will not stay put and the link will be useless. I learned the hard way. Watch carefully where the tiny cylindrical spacer goes and how it works.Solar watches are the way to go. My oldest solar watch is twelve years old and still works. I will never buy a battery operated watch, what a waste of money and time.I spend all day watching my watch. It is interesting observing the atmospheric pressure graph. It shows you the atmospheric fluctuations every two hours and displays it in a tiny graph in the watch. The temperature sensor is not very accurate if you leave the watch in your wrist. You can adjust the reading but you will have to read the big tiny manual to learn all the crystal ball's secrets.Enjoy it, it is a fun watch to own.

reviewText: I'm a runner and triathlete and was curious to see what kind of uses the Timex Ironman Road Trainer watch could be used for. I currently use a Garmin 610 (with HRM- heart rate monitor) for running and biking and a lesser version Timex watch for swimming. I was hopeful this would combine the information for all 3 sports while I'm saving for the Garmin 910.To start with the watch comes with a HRM and a strap and a very thick instruction booklet. Since I already owned/used a Timex watch for swimming, I was familiar with the settings. Even so, it took a bit of trial and error to set the time/date. The directions were not helpful in how to set the watch, especially since you have to use a button they don't refer to, to actually save the settings. It's not too hard to figure out but annoying that it's not intuitive or easy to follow the directions.Right away the wristband is stiff and difficult to manipulate. The watch face is also bigger than my other Timex but smaller than my current Garmin 610, to give some comparison. It makes a nice in between face size. The Timex works by storing "lap" data and displays the current lap number and time. Click the "mode" button and you are in the "chrono" setting - which is where the time and lap number is displayed.The stop/start and split buttons are pretty easy to find - the split button is the big pink one on the face. Sometimes while swimming I find the split button to be tricky though. I'm not sure how hard I have to push to record the lap but push too hard and it records more than one lap. So I usually waste several seconds (wait 8 seconds after pushing the split button and the time resumes while showing the lap number) to ensure I only pressed hard enough for one lap to be recorded.The pink Timex offers more options than my other one - namely interval timer and a heart rate monitor. The strap and monitor are built similar to my current Garmin one. The interval timer is meant to remind you of when to run intervals - or can remind you to eat/drink or any other alert you'd like. I find this a bit difficult to set but once I did it was a nice reminder if you want one. I found the Garmin settings easier and more intuitive but once I figured out the Timex ones they worked just fine.Now to the meat of the watch - the HRM. To use the strap you have to wet the plastic probes and place them on your diaphragm. This isn't a monitor of a wrist pulse. I found the Timex strap to be stiff and it chafed me badly. To be fair, I chafe easily but the Timex strap was so stiff I was almost bleeding. To see my HR I had to set it up on the watch and tell it what was a resting HR and recovery one. I already knew what my HR zones should be but the booklet offers no help there nor were the instructions that easy to follow when trying to do this. After a bit of messing up and wanting to throw the watch, I eventually figured it out.To see the HR while running or biking you have to push the HR button. It's not that big of a deal. The watch is also set up to beep at you when you're above or below your designated HR, which is nice. As a HRM it works decently and accurately, if a bit painfully due to chafing. However as a run or bike watch, I found it nearly worthless. It's not GPS based so it doesn't count laps while running or biking. You have to already know when you hit each mile and without a gps, how would you know that? It's just a timer, which is helpful when swimming but not helpful when running or biking if you're going for a certain distance. If you want to run or bike for a set time (say 30 minutes) then the timer may be more useful.Overall this watch's effectiveness and usefulness depends what you want it for. For serious runners/athletes I can't imagine it'll do much for them without the added GPS function. It's limited in the data it offers - timing mostly - so it limits the usefulness of the watch. I find it only useful for swimming. If a casual gym goer wants a HR monitor as the primary use, this could work but other than that it's a more expensive swim watch that offers interval alarms. At best it's a backup swim watch for me.
summary: Depends what you want to use it for...

reviewText: This is a good watch, when it it working.  The problem is that is keeps failing.  The time-keeping function is great.  The altimeter is also very good.  Like all altimeters, you must periodically adjust the height to account for changes in barometric pressure.  The compass is very hit and miss.  I have learned that this is generally the case on all watch compasses.  The compass is usually good enough to use, but not good enough to rely upon if you are out in the woods.  The reason for the two stars, is that I have had two identical fails of the lower button on the right side of the watch.  The watch stops processing any input from this button rendering the watch useless.  The first fail happened under warranty, and Suunto quickly replaced the watch with a new watch.  This is great customer service.  However, the replacement watch has now failed in the same way.  This makes it very hard to recommend this watch.
summary: Lower button on right side has failed in two different watches

description: The award-winning Suunto Core is a sophisticated outdoor instrument that gathers a range of data to help you navigate your way through the wilder parts of the world. The log recorder stores all your movements in altitude between the start and stop times, so you can find out how much you climbed, the duration of ascents and descents, average ascent and descent speed and more. Suunto Core displays the current sea level pressure as a detailed graph, showing recording of the last 24 hours with a recording interval of 30 minutes. The storm alarm notifies you of a sudden drop in air pressure, which may be related to worsening weather conditions. Suunto Core senses your movement or lack thereof, switching between altimeter and barometer accordingly. A drop in air pressure while you’re sleeping under the stars will be recorded for what it really is: a change in barometric pressure, not altitude. The digital compass displays the cardinal or half-cardinal point and the North. The declination adjustment function allows you to correct the difference between the true North and magnetic North. The Suunto Core provides current and maximum depth reached during your snorkeling dive. The maximum depth of the device is 10m (328 ft). Watch functions include time, dual time, date, alarm, sports chronograph, countdown timer and predicted times for sunrise and sunset for over 400 locations worldwide. reviewText: I've been a user of this watch since 93.  It may not have all the latest and greatest functions, but what it does have is very useful.Stopwatch with lap counter, a countdown feature, and two timezones.  It's also waterproof up to 100 meters.  The new watches have the indiglo thing, (mine had that tiny little lightbulb on the left that never quite lit up the whole screen).On some watches I've seen, setting the time, alarm, etc, have been very frustrating, trying to find the right combination of buttons to change things.  This watch is very simple.  Hold the 'set' button for a couple seconds until it starts blinking, then cycle through with 'mode'  All changes are instantaneous.  All the buttons are labled too.The only real beef I have is the watchband.  The belt loop seems rather fragile.  I've gone through several of these, and that little thing insists on breaking.  Otherwise the watch is durable.  I've lost count of all the times I've banged it hard against something, and it lived.  The covering is all scraped up, and the buttons are starting to corrode after all these years, but the thing still works.  That's far more than enough to make me a repeat customer.At the time of this review, Amazon has these listed for $37.99 before the "discount".  You can pick this up at Kmart or Walmart for $29
