reviewText: I previously owned theNew Balance Men's MR790 Running Shoe, which I very much enjoyed.  I don't actually run trail, I was just looking for a lightweight, capable shoe for everyday purposes that could also serve me for camping and impromptu sporting on grass and dirt.  The 790 fit the bill quite well.  The MT840 is slightly better in some areas and worse in others.The 790 is nearly devoid of cushioning, an issue which the 840 addresses in spades.  The insole is much more substantial and the extra-knobby outsole actually creates a bit of extra cush on hard surfaces while providing excellent grip on softer ground.  I find myself substantially agile on grass and dirt when playing frisbee.  The tread on the 790 tended to get rather slippery on wet concrete conditions, the 840 not so.  Also, while I initially assumed the N-Lock system was little more than a gimmick, it really does pull this shoe much more snugly around my foot.On the downside, these are heavier than the 790, though the 790 is probably the lightest shoe I've owned.  They fit substantially more snugly, which I'm sure delivers real benefit when running, but just creates a kind of foot fatigue by day's end.  I wouldn't call them uncomfortable, they're actually quite capable feeling on the foot, but when I get home, I'm ready to have them off.  If you're the type that wears shoes continually from awakening to bedtime, these may irritate you a little.In general, great shoe overall.

reviewText: As these shoes described to be for "Rain and Garden" shoes with all day comfort, that is what I thought I would get from these shoes. That's right!! That "all day comfort" consists of your feet sitting in water the entire time you wear them;  you literally "slosh" when you walk because your shoes are full of water.  Maybe they would make a better planter...but no, the plants would suffocate from lack of air and drainage.  It's a shame I cannot have faith in product made in the USA.  Please DO NOT WASTE YOUR HARD EARNED MONEY on the worst pair of gardening shoes ever invented - I don't know what they were made for, in fact.  If you want shoes for gardening or to keep your feet dry/protected from rain, THESE SHOES ARE NOT FOR YOU.  They literally fill with water and unless you remove the shoe and empty the water,  you will have plastic material (that cannot breath) around your foot that is filled with water that remains in the shoe for as long as you wear them.  With every sincerity, I am in no way exaggerating.  Although they are more expensive, stick with the Lewis Clark.  They may not have cute, fancy designs but they are a fantastic garden shoe that have a mesh material allowing the shoe to constantly drain from any water that may get in it and your feet to breath and truly stay comfortable, rather than keeping your feet water logged and miserable the longer you wear a Slogger. In addition, the sole on the Lewis & Clark's will last a life time with a fantastic grip; UNLIKE the Sloggers.  It's disgusting to have bought such a pitiful, misrepresented product.

reviewText: My daughter bought me this for my birthday. We're both avid runners and have been for years.  I spent hours finally getting it to record the distance "close" to an accurate reading.  I finally figured out that over-adjusting the calibration values would allow me to manipulate the result enough to "tweak" it to an accuracy level I could live with which was always at least .10 off a mile lower than it should be.  I prefered under recoding to over recording the run.  I also learned to live with knowing every 10 miles meant I ran at least 11 ;-(Then the software for loading the results stopped working.  I tried every suggestion but nothing worked.  I'm a computer professional so I'm sure the issue is either with the firmware or the USB connectors.  You can't update the firmware without the software working.  This is after only 2 months.Called Nike support for a refund and all they would offer me is another one.  I explained that I'm so unhappy that I just want a refund so I can buy a GPS watch instead but they don't offer refunds.  I called the store where it was bought and they have a no refund policy after 30 days.  I'm so dissatisfied that I'd rather not even bother with another even though it would be free.  Bought my daughter Garmin Forerunner 110 GPS-Enabled Unisex Sport Watch and she loves it.  Wish I could get a refund so I could buy one.

reviewText: This is the third F91W-1 watch that I have owned.  My  previous one still functions as a watch, but the band broke after I had worn it daily for two years.  I ordered a whole new watch because its Amazon price was only a little more than $10--about twice the cost of a replacement band from Amazon.The watch itself is great--5 stars.  This is a no-nonsense watch  which gives you the time, date, a stopwatch, and an alarm.  The functions are simple to access and the battery life is great.  I have worn it while sweating in the gym or working in the yard, and it seems to survive the perspiration just fine.The watch band doesn't last more than a couple of years, however--3 stars.  The long part that threads through the buckle cracks where it rests under the buckle.  I have tried replacing the band myself.  On the first occasion I was successful, but on the second I broke the watch case because I didn't have the correct tools.  If you buy the band in a store, the sales person may put the new band on for you, but you may pay more for the band than the cost of the new watch on Amazon.It's worth buying the watch.  How you deal with a broken band after two years is a toss-up.

Perhaps because it's such a heavy watch, the vibration is not s strong as some of the other VibraLite watches. We were considering just replacing the battery, but we just got it a few months ago and the rest of the watch works- when we go to set the alarm with sound it doesn't get messed up. No idea if ours is defective or if the watch as a whole is.

reviewText: I purchased the pebble not from amazon, but i'm an avid amazon customer.  I bought it for the intent of discreet notifications while i'm in meetings which can sometimes be all day.  The benefits just add on... using my HTC One Max android phone I was able to download Glance app as well as a couple other helpful apps like the dialer.  The other reviewers don't have it quite right that you can't text or call from the watch.  The watch itself may not have a speaker or mic, but with the dialer i can call out to whomever I would like within my contacts, or recent called list.  I can control volume, speakerphone, hang up and mute from my wrist while never touching the phone.  The Glance app is basically a separate UI for the watch.  It has some really nice built-in faces that includes Yahoo weather live updates (15 minutes).  It also provides the ability to text some canned replies.  Simple "Thanks!" or "love you!" or whatever you want to set up via your smart phone.  It also has a built in 7 day forecast.  The display is readable in any light and with a quick flip of the wrist it's got a backlight.  This watch will only improve with the release of the SDK 2.0 for those who like to code new apps for the pebble.  Only thing I wish it were a little better quality feeling, the plastic sides are slightly roughed.

reviewText: I have both this watch and theTraser T4004.357.37.01 Chrono Big Date Pro Blue, Chronograph Watch.  I like the Titanium version better but not because it's that much lighter.  In fact, it's not that much lighter.  This watch is 3.7 oz and the stainless version is 6 oz.  You notice the difference but it's not dramatic (to me).What I prefer is the finish of this watch.  It's a bit darker and a touch less shiny than the picture.  Also, there's nothing to wear away.  The only thing under the titanium is more titanium.Both watches have a couple other features I really like.  The minute hand for the stop watch goes to 30 minutes.  Other "three eye" watches track to an hour and for me it's difficult to see which minute it is.  In this case there is plenty of space between hash marks and the hand steps from one mark to halfway between to the next.  It can also do split times.  For me that's not a big deal but it's nice to have.And of course there's the Tritium.  You can easily read the time in any light, at any time, without having to depend on "charging" the luminescent material.  However, many of the marketing photos I've seen with this and other "tritium" watches do them a disservice.  The markings do not glow as brightly as they are sometimes depicted.  They are not bright enough to read the watch face, read a book, signal for help, or temporarily disorient an attacker.  They glow at a constant level, about as brightly as a "normal" watch somewhere between 10 and 30 minutes after it's been exposed to a bright light.  (Green tritium markings are perceived as glowing a bit brighter than blue ones and it's all in the same ballpark.)  For me, that is exactly what I want.

reviewText: As my vision deteriorates, I've been forced into progressive lenses and that present a problem using my camera's view finder, especially in bright sunlight. My routine is to whip off my sunglasses, jam them in my mouth, then frame the image thru the VF. Sweaty sunglasses with sunscreen on the bows are pretty disgusting (yuk!). And flip-up clip-on sunglasses over my prescription clear glasses leave my face spaced too far away from the view finder: my camera's EVF senses sunlight and assume I'm not using the EVF (annoying!).The Hoodman PhotoFrames, with a few whines, pretty much solves my problem. I bought lenses at LensCrafter (their prices have exploded!) and had them mount the lenses in my Hoodman frames. The end product functions very well: I can walk around with corrected sun glasses, then when I see a shot it just takes a quick lift of my right lens using the corner of the camera as I bring it to my eye and I'm in business.As I said, I have a few whines:- the lens retainers (the metal loop that surrounds the prescription lens to hold it in place) are shaped for clear vision or far sighted corrective lenses. Post-cataract surgery, my vision is near sighted. So my lenses don't fit the frame very well because they have more curvature. The fit is close enough to retain the lenses, but it sure looks precarious.- as another poster says, the hinge doesn't have much friction; if your prescription lenses are heavy (maybe polarized lenses which are laminated), the lens can flop away from your face when you lower your head. There is no adjustment to pre-set friction and no detent stop.- I love the loops that fit over the ears because they keep the glasses on my face when my hands are occupied; others may not feel the same way.- the typical range of frame sizing (pupil spacing, bow length, and lens-holder curvature) is not available- the one-size-fits-all approach is unfortunate. In my case the bows are a few millimeters too long, but not too long to make the frames unusable.On the plus side,- the frames are light weight and comfortable;- the loops retain the glasses when active;- my EVF doesn't see enough light to cause it to shut off the EVF display; and most important- they do the job! I can flip the lens out of the way easily without losing the setup I'm trying to frame.I gave a 4-star rating because of the one-size-fits-all limitation and the lack of friction adjustment (or alternately a detent).With respect to doing their intended job, however, they are an excellent (and apparently the *only*) choice for eye glass-wearers. (You who wear contacts are to be envied as there are less expensive solutions.)
summary: Finally I can use the view finder easily!

reviewText: I bought this band for my Citizen dive watch. At work I need to write and type on a computer - who doesn't? So the bulky rubber strap that came with the Citizen had to go.I have not yet had The Band on for an hour and already I can tell this was a good purchase. Some initial observations:1. "The Band" is thin enough to write and type with comfortably. Good for us Jacques Cousteau IT types.2. Unlike some Velcro watch band designs, "The Band" does not use a ring to pull the band back towards you. You simply wrap "The Band" twice around your wrist.3. As others have said, learning how to wrap "The Band" on is a little tricky. If you have ever wrapped an Ace bandage around your wrist, the procedure is very similar to that. You know how hard it can be to get that initial snug wrap? Same thing with "The Band". I can see how the process will be frustrating in the morning when I am in a hurry. Oh well...score one for the ring style bands that go on very quickly.4. The instructions say to slide your watch to the end of the narrow strap until your watch is up against the wide part of the band. I found this put a lot of stress on the watch spring bar and was uncomfortable to wear. Sliding the watch back so there was about a 1/2" of narrow band between my watch and the wide part of the band fixed the problem. The above will not really make sense until you wrap "The Band" on with your watch and see how it feels. Expect to do some adjusting until everything is comfortable based upon your wrist and watch style.5. For a large dive or tachy-whatever watch, the wide band makes a nice stable "platform."6. As others have mentioned, this is a casual watch band. Depending upon your line of work, it may not be suitable. This is not a criticism just an observation. A Patek Phillippe would not be suitable on the beach where "The Band" would be.Overall I am pleased with the purchase. It will just take some time to learning how to put "The Band" on my wrist.
summary: Wear a dive watch, need to type and write? This band works.

reviewText: I have a Casio HD watch I picked up about seven years ago or thereabouts. The watch face reads "TEN YEAR BATTERY" in small but earnest "bank it" type, so it's still ticking along just fine. However, the watch band had disintegrated a year or two into wearing it, I expect because I was wearing it in Houston heat, and coating it with my Houston sweat. (You'll never guess where I was living when I wore this watch.)Anyway, very recently I realized I still had this watch sitting around, and it was still ticking, so I figured I'd check Amazon to see if I could find a replacement band. It was ridiculously easy to find, particularly since the model number for the band is embossed on both pieces. While unnecessary, the watch repair kit I'd purchased about the same time came in handy for replacing the broken bits of the old wristband with this new one. I could've just as easily used a pocketknife to release the spring-loaded wristband pegs, but I rather like using the right tool for the job. (Make of that what you will.)Of course, being brand new, the band has a tendency to lie flat; I'm wearing the watch even now, in an effort to "train" the band to be more curled. Hardly a deal-breaker; just a personal preference.

I am hoping this is fixed now, as I didn't have the problem with the previous 7 watches I owned.I've used this style of watch for the past 10 years.  I can't find another watch that has the features as well as the small face so I keep buying it. (If anyone knows of another watch please let me know). My husband went through a bunch of more expensive Nike watches that also broke after a year or, so I figure spending $50 a yar for a watch is better than $100.  It is a shame because I know Timex knows how to make watches that last.  The same friend mentioned above had a Timex that she bought 20 years ago that lasted for 10 years, with replaceable bands, all the features, and a small face, but they no longer make that model. title: Suunto X-Lander Wrist-Top Computer Watch with Altimeter, Barometer, Compass, and Chronograph
description: The ultimate option for the outdoor enthusiast, the silver Suunto X-Lander wrist-top computer offers an accurate altimeter, a complete barometer, a precise electronic compass, and a multifunction sports watch in a single elegant package. Regardless of your excursion--whether it's climbing mountains, riding a muddy bike track, or skiing off piste--you need accurate, real-time information about your surroundings to pull off a successful trip. The X-Lander contributes by not only providing important data, but also keeping track of your activities so you can make rational decisions at key moments. In addition, the watch is user-friendly and solidly built, with a non-allergenic aluminum casing, a carbon-fiber back, a durable mineral crystal glass, and a water-resistant fabric strap.The built-in altimeter, which boasts a range of up to 29,500 feet, puts all 14 of the world's 8,000-plus-meter summits within the avid climber's range. Among the altimeter's functions are an altitude measurement function that lets you follow the vertical progress between stages, an automatic 24-hour memory that stores the altitude and ascent/decent rate for every hour, and an adjustable altitude alarm. Climbers will also dig the logbook function, which lets you record total and cumulative vertical ascents and descents as well as the number of runs skied.The X-Lander also displays the current barometric pressure and temperature--a must for activities in which weather plays a factor. The device automatically records barometric data for the previous four days, with the first six hours manifested in one-hour intervals and the rest in six-hour intervals. When the reference altitude is set correctly, the instrument also displays the present sea level pressure, which makes it easier to read and understand the barometric pressure at high altitudes.And few things are more important when exploring unfamiliar territory than a compass. reviewText: [UPDATE]At the time I wrote this review, I had only worn the rainpants for a short time in a moderate rain.  Last week I wore them in a downpour for an hour on the freeway.  They do leak in the middle, not a lot - my jeans were damp rather than soaked.  But it they were distinctly uncomfortable for that part of the ride.  Rainpants costing over $100 shouldn't leak at all.  I suspect that you could treat them with seam sealer and plug the leak - but seam sealer wears out after a while & you'll only notice when you get that cold trickle "down there."[ORIGINAL REVIEW]Here in Seattle, you've only got two choices: either you ride in the rain or you ride in August.  Rainsuits are more popular than sunglasses.  Not sure how it happened, but my old pair of neoprene rain pants shrunk over the summer.  Needed a new pair, did my homework & decided on the Icon Pdx's.The ads are right: these don't suck.  They're very well made, lots of adjustment straps, etc.  The zippers are all the nearly-waterproof type, well protected by flies.  All the snaps, straps, zippers, toggles, etc are big enough to use while wearing gloves.  Overall construction leads me to believe they'd take a lot of abuse (AKA "real life") without a problem.The stirrups are removable, I like that - stirrups are a bit of a pain, and the Pdx's legs have drawstrings on the bottom which keep the pants from riding up in the wind anyway.The legs are long enough for a tall guy with his legs stretched out.  The pants are fully lined with a breathable mesh that should keep them (and me) from sweating.  The outer pockets are as close to waterproof as you can get while still allowing easy access, a little on the narrow side though.  I can't get my paws into 'em even without my gloves on.Two nits keeps this from being a five-star review:They're a little tight in the waist for 2X's - oh, they go around my ample middle with a little slack, and they've got room for my chaps - however they're not big enough to go over my leather jacket. I prefer bibs that are sized to go over my jacket, but they work well enough with a waterproof over-jacket on top.Nit Number two is the supposed reflective graphics.  There are only a couple, they're small, and both of them are Icons.  errr, I mean "graphical representations of the company name" (which just happens to be 'Icon.')  One of them is basically in my lap & if a car's headlights can actually hit it I'm probably no longer shiny side up.I'd prefer some reflective stripes instead, and I really don't like having a lot of logos pasted all over my body.  If they want me to endorse their product, they can talk to my agent, same as anybody else.  ::cough::

reviewText: This is a good watch just for basic every day use.  I would NOT recommend it for someone that wants to use it for running or tri training IF you are over 40 and need reading glasses for small print. If you need reading glasses and have not used this particular watch before, the small print around the inside edge of the glass is very difficult or near impossible to read - without glasses - which you will not have while running or swimming.  Some of the lap times and other things are also difficult to read, especially while you are out running and are looking at the numbers on the fly.  Also, the layout of the functions and which buttons do what has never seemed intuitive to me on this particular model.  With some functions the 2 buttons on the right side do the same thing and you must press a button on the top left to get to a function that you need.  It's more difficult to press the button on the top left side while you are running, especially if you wear the band a little loose.  When you press the buttons on the left side with the band not fastened super tight, then the whole watch shifts on your arm which makes it seem like you have to chase it down your arm til it hits your wrist bone to catch it.  There are 4 buttons on the sides plus the large button on the bottom of the face.  Don't know why they couldn't have just shifted some of the functions to work with the other buttons available.  Just not a great design.Also, the band on this watch is molded onto the watch.  If your band breaks you will not be able to replace just the band.  The whole watch will be garbage.  The basic time, date, alarm is all fine for every day use.  For running or tri training I would recommend shopping around for something else, especially if you are someone who wears reading glasses these days.  I've noticed some of the other models do have print now around the face of the watch on the outside of the glass area.  I'm looking into some of those now just for running.  This one I will continue to use just for every day wear.  But for running I will be looking into getting some other model, and may have to go with a larger Men's model just to get numbers that are easier to read while running even though I would prefer a Women's model.  They just don't seem to make some of the Women's models with all the goodies that the men's models get or they make the numbers cramped to fit into the smaller face.Overall, good watch for basic every day use.  Not so good for running and not so good for over 40 eyesight.  Design with some functions really could be better.

reviewText: I really like my Pathfinder. It has great looks, large digital display which is perfect for aging eyes. Fantastic colour of the Titanium case and strap, which brings me to my pet peeve..the bloody strap scratches up really easily! I've had a TAG for coming on 25 years now, and the steel strap still looks amazing, and I wear it all-day long, doing everything from working on my car to working at my desk.My Titanium strap is all scratched up already from less than one month of use...and all the scratches seem to come from regular use at the desk! I'm a graphics artist and of course, my hands are sliding up and down between keyboard to trackball to digital table the whole day...more than your average user. However, against a smooth wooden surface it can get scratched? I never thought that would happen!Its a pity though, as I really find the Titanium colour and look to be truly beautiful for a watch. But if you use this watch like its intended to be used, be aware that the surface scratches easily.I took the watch hunting with me the other day, and it worked really well for predicting sunrise/sunset times, which are critical for hunters. The temperature feature was also really helpful..at least in confirming why it was so cold up knee-deep in snow! I did find it worked pretty good in the hot tub as well, as it gave a pretty good indication of the underwater temps of the tub. The barometer was equally good at predicting bad weather. I wasn't too sure about the Altimeter though it showed I was 860m up a mountain at one point.All-in, I would've given this watch 4 stars or even 5 if not for the pain I feel now looking at the strap. For what its worth, if you're not staring at the watch close up, you would probably not notice the scratches on the strap. Under bright light though, they do show up, as shiny streaks against the matt surface of the strap.

reviewText: These are pretty solid all-around climbing shoes, especially if you value comfort and wearability over super-high performance.  They are very stylish--I love the red color--and unusually comfortable for climbing shoes.  There was literally no break-in period, and right out of the box I could wear them for hours without any discomfort.  They are cushier and more sneaker-like than many other climbing shoes.  I would recommend them, especially for a first pair of climbing shoes, or for anyone who wants comfortable shoes with decent performance that they can stand in all day.  But I don't love them as much as I wanted to.  For comfort, I still actually prefer my worn old Five Ten Spires, and for performance I prefer my new La Sportiva Katana Lace-Ups.Good stuff:ComfortStyleDecent but not spectacular climbing performanceNot so good stuff:Stiffness--These shoes are kind of stiff, and less flexible than I want them to be.  I slip more than in my old shoes because I can't feel the rock as well with my toes.Stickiness--The rubber on these is not quite as sticky as the Stealth C4 rubber on my old Spires.  (Still good, but not as good).Breathability--These are lined and made of synthetic material, so they are hotter and less breathable than the butter-soft unlined suede of my old Five Ten Spires.  The Spires conformed perfectly to my foot after a while, and I don't think the Sirens will do that.Performance--There's always a trade-off between comfort and performance.  These are fine, but they are not great for toe-hooks and they are not great for overhangs.  If you are a beginner, you probably won't care about that.  I don't love them for smearing either.  If you're looking for more aggressive shoes to push you to the next level, I'd go with the La Sportiva Katanas--but they are more expensive and much harder to break in.I saw that some other people have complained about durability.  I haven't had any problems with that so far, but I have only been climbing in these for about a month (twice a week).Bottom line:  If you're going with comfort and wearability over really high performance, you will not be sorry to buy these shoes.  But I'd really recommend checking out the Five Ten Spires, which I actually prefer because they are stickier, more breathable, more flexible, and really long-lasting even if they are not as pretty.  If you're going for high performance, you may want something with a more aggressive (and less comfortable) shape.Sizing:  If you're buying these shoes, you're probably picking comfort over performance, so it doesn't seem worth it to put yourself through agony to try to wear shoes that are way too small.  I did originally try a half size smaller than my normal street shoe size and climbed in them about 3 times before realizing that the synthetic material just wasn't stretching.  Now I have my normal street shoe size, and the fit is just right.
summary: Wearable right out of the box

title: Suunto X-Lander Wrist-Top Computer Watch with Altimeter, Barometer, Compass, and Chronograph
description: The ultimate option for the outdoor enthusiast, the silver Suunto X-Lander wrist-top computer offers an accurate altimeter, a complete barometer, a precise electronic compass, and a multifunction sports watch in a single elegant package. Regardless of your excursion--whether it's climbing mountains, riding a muddy bike track, or skiing off piste--you need accurate, real-time information about your surroundings to pull off a successful trip. The X-Lander contributes by not only providing important data, but also keeping track of your activities so you can make rational decisions at key moments. In addition, the watch is user-friendly and solidly built, with a non-allergenic aluminum casing, a carbon-fiber back, a durable mineral crystal glass, and a water-resistant fabric strap.The built-in altimeter, which boasts a range of up to 29,500 feet, puts all 14 of the world's 8,000-plus-meter summits within the avid climber's range. Among the altimeter's functions are an altitude measurement function that lets you follow the vertical progress between stages, an automatic 24-hour memory that stores the altitude and ascent/decent rate for every hour, and an adjustable altitude alarm. Climbers will also dig the logbook function, which lets you record total and cumulative vertical ascents and descents as well as the number of runs skied.The X-Lander also displays the current barometric pressure and temperature--a must for activities in which weather plays a factor. The device automatically records barometric data for the previous four days, with the first six hours manifested in one-hour intervals and the rest in six-hour intervals. When the reference altitude is set correctly, the instrument also displays the present sea level pressure, which makes it easier to read and understand the barometric pressure at high altitudes.And few things are more important when exploring unfamiliar territory than a compass. The X-Lander's electronic compass contributes by guiding you with cardinal or half- cardinal points and a North-South arrow. The compass can also be set to track a certain bearing, which helps you follow a chosen direction. Meanwhile, the unit's declination adjustment function allows you to correct the difference between true North and magnetic North.In addition to the variety of outdoor functions, the X-Lander also displays normal time, with such add-ons as three daily alarms, a calendar programmed to the year 2089, a stopwatch with split-time measurement, and a countdown timer. Other features include a durable negative LCD display, a user-replaceable battery, and water-resistance to 100 feet. The X-Lander is backed by a two-year warranty on parts and labor.What's in the Box?X-Lander wrist-top computer, battery, user's manual.

reviewText: I've had my Suunto Core Regular Black for over six months, having purchased it used from an eBay auction in June 2013.  I am a watch fanatic, and I was impressed by the Core's large digital display, so, when I found a good deal, I snatched it up.  Although the Core is a fantastic watch for all its functions, as I work in law enforcement, on patrol, I need a watch that does some things that the Core does not.  Here is my critique of the Suunto Core, positive and otherwise, with respect to its use as a duty watch, after my having worn it exclusively for the last six months.The Suunto Core is a large watch, with a 50mm diameter, and it has a very uncluttered display, with a lot of empty space.  It is appealing to look at and definitely exudes a tough, cool character.  After six months of wearing it, I have yet to scratch the crystal or rub off more than a few tiny dots on the outside edges of the bezel.  This is a rugged watch.  It looks like a cop watch and probably draws the same kind of attention that my cargo pants do when I wear either off-duty.All watch bands should be as nice as the Suunto Core's.  The silicone band blends with the watch nicely, and the five serrations on both sides of the band have a gentle curve that compliments the curvature of the bezel.  The buckle is excellent, with rounded edges and a tongue that is 1 cm wide and snuggles into the frame effortlessly.  The holes in the band are perfectly spaced, and the retention band for the strap has a small tooth that snaps into place, securely preventing the strap from coming loose, something that I have yet to see on any other watch band.  The band is quite soft, especially in comparison to Casio bands, and it hugs my wrist snugly without being uncomfortable, restraining the watch from twisting out of position on my wrist.In daylight and indoors, the Core's digital display is the easiest to read of any digital watch I own, and that includes Casio G-Shocks and Pathfinders.  The time display numerals at 1 cm are nearly twice as big as those on my Casio Pathfinder (6mm).  Even at an extreme angle, where the LCD turns from its light grey background to the purple-green haze, it's very easy to read the time.  At night, as long as there is just a little bit of ambient light, such as vehicle headlights, overhead street light, or a full moon, the display can be read a lot more easily than my Casio's.That being said, it makes me wonder why Suunto could not develop a decent electroluminescent (EL) display, as it is a pale, dim green, which makes it difficult to read quickly.  Casio backlights are far superior to Suunto's in terms of brightness and color.  Even in a well-lit indoor room, I can see the Casio's green glow and read the display still; on the Suunto, I will not see the EL at all, and the digital numerals will be washed out, which is odd.  The Suunto Core also lacks an automated electroluminescent function, so I have to push a button in order to light up the face, rather than have it automatically activate as I roll my wrist over in the natural motion of viewing a wristwatch.Although I have yet to replace the battery, I know the Core is energy hungry, which may be why the time needs to be corrected regularly, once a month.  I don't think a digital watch should be off by an entire minute after sixty days, but my Suunto is.  I was spoiled by my Casios that received an atomic clock signal from Fort Collins, Colorado, but even my Casio Pathfinder that does not have this function is only off by mere seconds every year.  Luckily, replacing a CR2032 on the Suunto is an easy task.The Suunto will display time in hours and minutes, but does not allow for a 24-hour time readout.  Also, if I want seconds displayed as numerals, then the date will not be displayed, as these functions use the same line on the LCD.  There is a digital second hand, but it turns off after a few minutes and needs to be reactivated by pushing the light button, which is irritating.  Since I often need to get time in hours, minutes, and seconds at a moment's glance on duty, this is a dealbreaker for me.I like the myriad functions Suunto has programmed into the Core, such as the sunrise-sunset predictor, the superbly accurate altimeter and barometer, and the large compass display, but I rarely use them.  Suunto wasn't trying to make a military or law enforcement watch with the Core.  While I can recommend the Suunto Core in general as an excellent, rugged digital watch, I would not use it on-duty because of the shortcomings I've listed.
summary: Superb Watch But Not the Best Choice for Law Enforcement Use
title: Suunto Men's SS014809000 Core Outdoor Matrix Regular Black Watch
description: The award-winning Suunto Core is a sophisticated outdoor instrument that gathers a range of data to help you navigate your way through the wilder parts of the world. The altimeter features a range up to 9000m (29500 ft) and sports an altitude difference measurement that allows you to track your progress in terms of altitude climbed. The log recorder stores all your movements in altitude between the start and stop times, so you can find out how much you climbed, the duration of ascents and descents, average ascent and descent speed and more. Suunto Core displays the current sea level pressure as a detailed graph, showing recording of the last 24 hours with a recording interval of 30 minutes. The storm alarm notifies you of a sudden drop in air pressure, which may be related to worsening weather conditions. Suunto Core senses your movement or lack thereof, switching between altimeter and barometer accordingly. A drop in air pressure while you’re sleeping under the stars will be recorded for what it really is: a change in barometric pressure, not altitude. The digital compass displays the cardinal or half-cardinal point and the North. The declination adjustment function allows you to correct the difference between the true North and magnetic North. The Suunto Core provides current and maximum depth reached during your snorkeling dive. The maximum depth of the device is 10m (328 ft). Watch functions include time, dual time, date, alarm, sports chronograph, countdown timer and predicted times for sunrise and sunset for over 400 locations worldwide. Also features a digital thermometer. Menu-based user interface in English, German, French and Spanish. 2 year warranty.

title: Suunto Core Black Military
description: Building on the success of the venerable Suunto Vector, the Suunto Core keeps you informed of conditions while you hike, bike, or camp, making it a terrific companion for outdoor enthusiasts of all stripes. What can the Suunto Core do for you? For starters, it can sense an approaching squall even when the sky looks clear. This intelligent Storm Alarm--one of several intelligent features designed to keep you safe and secure--is activated by a rapid drop in air pressure over a three-hour period. Once the Core senses the change, the Storm Alarm sounds and flashes, letting you know that something unpleasant is fast approaching. The built-in altimeter, meanwhile, displays your current elevation, shows how much you've climbed or descended, and records your entire session for later analysis. Accurate to within 30,000 feet, the altimeter is an extremely valuable tool for mountaineering, backcountry skiing, and wilderness travel. Add in such features as a barometer, a digital thermometer, a weather trend indicator, and a digital compass and you have a terrific wrist-top computer for almost all your outdoor needs. Additional features include several traditional watch functions, including dual times, a date display, and an alarm; predicted times for sunrise and sunset to help you maximize your daylight hours; an automatic Alti/Baro mode that senses movement or lack thereof and switches between the altimeter and barometer accordingly; a depth meter that provides accurate water depth readings to 30 feet; and the ability to function in English, German, French, and Spanish. The Suunto Core carries a two-year warranty.

description: The original Neoprene Eyewear Retainer -- patented in 1978 -- remains one of Croakies' most popular models. Made of snug-fitting, grippy neoprene material, its ends tightly grip your frames, so while you may lose yourself in your favorite activity, your glasses will remain securely strapped to your head.DetailsMade of durable HyPUR-cel neopreneColorfast and washableTwo inches of adjustmentFits most framesMade in the USAAbout CroakiesIn 1977, a local ski patrolman from Jackson Hole Mountain Resort in Wyoming came up with an idea for an eyewear retainer that would grip his shades through all kinds of alpine adventures. Using an old wetsuit and some sharp scissors, he made the first pair of eyewear retainers. The ingenious device was based on the design of a Chinese finger trap, and quickly became a hit with local ski patrolers. Demand picked up quickly for the patrolman's invention, which was initially nameless. Back in the seventies, the Jackson Hole ski patrol used the nickname "croakies" when they couldn't think of a word (think "thing- amajig"), but it finally stuck on the world'd first neoprene eyewear retainer.Croakies headquarters are still in Jackson Hole, with production in Bozeman, Montana. The inspiration remains the same -- to create eyewear retainers and accessories that provide comfort, style, durability, and functionality to active people of all ages. Croakies products are sold by retailers throughout the United States and in over 30 countries around the world. They've even been used out of this world, having become standard issue on the Space Shuttle in 1990.

reviewText: Updated Review:I was a bit hasty in my previous review.  It turns out that due to some confusion between Amazon's ordering system and the seller's system what I received was actually a woman's US size 9.  Shoemania quickly and politely corrected the problem, emailing me a prepaid return label and sent off another in the correct size.  Though they forgot to honor the 2-day shipping agreement they promptly credited me the price difference.  I've had a few weeks to try these sandals now and I like them very much.  I bought them to replace my beloved Mephistos which I had for years and had worn threadbare.  I'm diabetic and have problems wearing most other tighter fitting shoes so sandals tend to be my footwear of choice.These sandals do take some getting use to - they're a lot like walking on cushy rockers.  This makes it more comfortable to walk as the sandals rock forward with you in natural walking motion.  It is possible, however, to accidentally rock backwards far enough to fall backwards, so some care is necessary.  They are comfortable enough to wear all day and on extended walking tours.  One nit is that the strap that goes across the instep tends to push into your foot causing a little discomfort.  This is unavoidable as a result of the walking/rocking motion that is the point of the design.  Another nit is that the clips that secure the straps are a bit small and they're a little difficult to maneuver.  Overall, though, they are an excellent product - well made.  They still don't beat my beloved Mephistos, but they are 2/3 the price and a fine replacement.Previous Review:I wish I could comment on this sandal for its comfort and ergonomic design, but I am unable to squeeze into this very expensive miniature to be able to tell.  When I opened the box I immediately noticed the size problem and checked the markings on the heel strap - European size 40 1/3, US size 9.5.  Puzzled, as the sandals are significantly smaller than my other size 9.5 shoes, I took them to my friend at Nordstrom who measured them with his spiffy meter.  European size 38.5 / US size 8.  That seems more like it.  Why such a significant difference?  Have they no quality control?  For as expensive as these sandals were I expect much better.

reviewText: I have had a large bust all my life. I had owned a Title IX bra that I bought in 2006. Obviously, 7 years is way too long to have the same sports bra. I had read so many good things about the Enell bra and was really impressed by the beginnings of this bra company. If this bra was designed by a bustier woman with busty women in mind, I was willing to try it. I purchased a size 3. It fits well. It's possibly a touch too loose but I can't imagine going down a size. I feel well-supported in this bra!I love how this bra fits. I don't mind taking time to fasten it up because I know once on, nothing is going anywhere. I can't explain how incredible it felt to run -- REALLY run, without pain -- for the first time in years.Enell has created an exceptional product. Not only would I recommend it to all the well-endowed women I know, I've already done so!

reviewText: Although I have a smart phone, HRMs with all the bells and whistles don't appeal to me all that much. I was gifted this Timex model because I was sick of my MiO HRM (with a strap). I've used it several times so far and I love it.Pros:- The heart rate signal gets sent to the watch within seconds. I've seen the reviews that say it takes 10-15 minutes (so the user begins to sweat) but I just put it on dry and haven't had an issue.- The strap is extremely comfortable to wear. Just be mindful that you *can* undo the strap so that it's easier to put on. I learned after using the product for a few weeks.- You can alter the display to suit your needs. Meaning it can either display your actual heart rate or % of your max (either pre determined or set to what you want).- See the stock photo of the watch? With the heart rate range in smaller font and the time in the larger font? You can switch that around as well. Nice touch!Cons (minus 1 star):- Watch is a bit bulky- The start/split button below the face of the watch sometimes gets hit automatically as I'm hitting the weights. I imagine runners would *not* encounter this issue.- Only your last workout is stored in the watch. It is deleted when you start a new workout.I've owned a Reebok HRM (w/strap) and it crapped out after a few years and also a MiO HRM (w/strap) that never really worked correctly from the start. This, by and large, is my favorite HRM that I've used.Highly, highly recommended.
summary: No unnecessary features + simple to use = Great heart rate monitor!

The X-Lander contributes by not only providing important data, but also keeping track of your activities so you can make rational decisions at key moments. In addition, the watch is user-friendly and solidly built, with a non-allergenic aluminum casing, a carbon-fiber back, a durable mineral crystal glass, and a water-resistant fabric strap.The built-in altimeter, which boasts a range of up to 29,500 feet, puts all 14 of the world's 8,000-plus-meter summits within the avid climber's range. Among the altimeter's functions are an altitude measurement function that lets you follow the vertical progress between stages, an automatic 24-hour memory that stores the altitude and ascent/decent rate for every hour, and an adjustable altitude alarm. Climbers will also dig the logbook function, which lets you record total and cumulative vertical ascents and descents as well as the number of runs skied.The X-Lander also displays the current barometric pressure and temperature--a must for activities in which weather plays a factor. The device automatically records barometric data for the previous four days, with the first six hours manifested in one-hour intervals and the rest in six-hour intervals. When the reference altitude is set correctly, the instrument also displays the present sea level pressure, which makes it easier to read and understand the barometric pressure at high altitudes.And few things are more important when exploring unfamiliar territory than a compass. The X-Lander's electronic compass contributes by guiding you with cardinal or half- cardinal points and a North-South arrow. The compass can also be set to track a certain bearing, which helps you follow a chosen direction. Meanwhile, the unit's declination adjustment function allows you to correct the difference between true North and magnetic North.In addition to the variety of outdoor functions, the X-Lander also displays normal time, with such add-ons as three daily alarms, a calendar programmed to the year 2089, a stopwatch with split-time measurement, and a countdown timer. Other features include a durable negative LCD display, a user-replaceable battery, and water-resistance to 100 feet. The X-Lander is backed by a two-year warranty on parts and labor.What's in the Box?X-Lander wrist-top computer, battery, user's manual.

reviewText: This watch is what any practical outdoors person would want. First, it has style. This watch carries a statement that you are more practical than flashy, but not in a cheap way that other watches seem to portray. Second, it has several practical tools. It has a built-in digital compass, barometer, and altimeter. I haven't stress tested it, but it is fairly accurate after calibration. (You should read the manual). The compass is a bit sensitive to distortion from other metals/electronics, so best be careful and check twice. Third, it has a good weight, not too heavy, but not too light that I feel it's fragile. I've bumped it against several tables and surfaces but so far has held up quite well.On the negative side, first, it's a bit on the pricier side than a Timex or a G-Shock, but you are paying to differentiate. The Suunto brand name and the black-face watch design definitely stop G-Shock fans to ask what this watch is. Additionally, the Suunto core just doesn't carry the same feel. If you compare these side-by-side, this is bolder, hands down. Second, the wrist band is a bit hard to use. Once I put it on, it's difficult to take off. Not sure if any other owners have the same issue. Maybe this is why there are so many Suunto X-lander wrist bands for sale? When frustrated, it is hard to control the desire to rip it off your wrist.In summary, a great watch for functionality and style. It is THE watch to have if you are out in the wilderness or if GPS goes down. Yes, I rely on my iphone for GPS and google maps, but this is a great backup.Also, be careful that the seller doesn't sell you the non-black version. title: Suunto X-Lander Wrist-Top Computer Watch with Altimeter, Barometer, Compass, and Chronograph
description: The ultimate option for the outdoor enthusiast, the silver Suunto X-Lander wrist-top computer offers an accurate altimeter, a complete barometer, a precise electronic compass, and a multifunction sports watch in a single elegant package. Regardless of your excursion--whether it's climbing mountains, riding a muddy bike track, or skiing off piste--you need accurate, real-time information about your surroundings to pull off a successful trip. The X-Lander contributes by not only providing important data, but also keeping track of your activities so you can make rational decisions at key moments. In addition, the watch is user-friendly and solidly built, with a non-allergenic aluminum casing, a carbon-fiber back, a durable mineral crystal glass, and a water-resistant fabric strap.The built-in altimeter, which boasts a range of up to 29,500 feet, puts all 14 of the world's 8,000-plus-meter summits within the avid climber's range. Among the altimeter's functions are an altitude measurement function that lets you follow the vertical progress between stages, an automatic 24-hour memory that stores the altitude and ascent/decent rate for every hour, and an adjustable altitude alarm. Climbers will also dig the logbook function, which lets you record total and cumulative vertical ascents and descents as well as the number of runs skied.The X-Lander also displays the current barometric pressure and temperature--a must for activities in which weather plays a factor. The device automatically records barometric data for the previous four days, with the first six hours manifested in one-hour intervals and the rest in six-hour intervals. When the reference altitude is set correctly, the instrument also displays the present sea level pressure, which makes it easier to read and understand the barometric pressure at high altitudes.And few things are more important when exploring unfamiliar territory than a compass. The X-Lander's electronic compass contributes by guiding you with cardinal or half- cardinal points and a North-South arrow. The compass can also be set to track a certain bearing, which helps you follow a chosen direction. Meanwhile, the unit's declination adjustment function allows you to correct the difference between true North and magnetic North.In addition to the variety of outdoor functions, the X-Lander also displays normal time, with such add-ons as three daily alarms, a calendar programmed to the year 2089, a stopwatch with split-time measurement, and a countdown timer. Other features include a durable negative LCD display, a user-replaceable battery, and water-resistance to 100 feet. The X-Lander is backed by a two-year warranty on parts and labor.What's in the Box?X-Lander wrist-top computer, battery, user's manual.

title: Casio PRW 3000 Watch
description: The Casio PRW 3000 Watch won't cook your dinner, carry your gear, or give you a foot rub after a long hike, but it'll do just about everything else you can imagine on your next trek, backpacking trip, sailing mission, or time-traveling adventure. This little aluminum, resin, and mineral glass case packs a mind-boggling array of tech tools, from an altimeter to a barometer to a compass to a thermometer, all run by a solar-powered battery that'll last for up to seven months on a single charge. The altimeter, which measures in precise one-meter increments, has automatic and manual logging functions and can hold up to 30 records of high/low altitudes, cumulative ascent and descent, with a range from -2,300 to over 32,000 feet. That's just the beginning. The PRW 3000 has a barometer as well, which has an automatic pressure-change indicator to alert you to sudden swings, along with a pressure tendency graph and pressure differential graphic to give you a longer-term idea of what the weather's doing. To keep you on course, the compass has a graphic 16-point display for one-glance orientation, a bearing memory to keep you on route, and declination adjustment so your bearing is accurate no matter where in the world you are. We haven't even mentioned the one thing the PRW 3000's designed to do first and foremost--tell the time. It receives six atomic signals a day to ensure you're always on time, has 12- and 24-hour displays and five alarms so you never miss a mealtime, and sunset/sunrise, time zone, and calendar data. There isn't even space to discuss the stopwatch, 100m waterproofing, automatic LED, power-save function, or battery-life indicator, but trust that they're there.

reviewText: I've owned several heart rate monitors over the years. Especially for middle aged and older athletes, an HRM can inform you with great precision whether you are in your aerobic "zone" or how much under or over it you are. I have abandoned all my fancy bike computers and rely on my excellent Timex watch with HR display to get a good workout without having to track an array of stats.My original Timex strap, even with new battery, became unable to communicate with the watch for longer and longer periods of time until it became useless. This new strap worked fine right away. Follow the tips below to get good results from your HR strap:- Replace the C0232 battery every three months.- Coat the strap's receiver zones with a thin film of Spectra 36O Electrode Gel. This works far better at maintaining a good connection than does spit or hair gel.- Position the strap a little further down your rib cage than seems ideal. For me, having the center of the strap just below my sternum works best. If you start losing the signal during a ride or run, grab the middle of the strap from outside your shirt and position it a little higher or lower.Happy aerobic exercising!

title: Suunto X-Lander Wrist-Top Computer Watch with Altimeter, Barometer, Compass, and Chronograph
description: The ultimate option for the outdoor enthusiast, the silver Suunto X-Lander wrist-top computer offers an accurate altimeter, a complete barometer, a precise electronic compass, and a multifunction sports watch in a single elegant package. Regardless of your excursion--whether it's climbing mountains, riding a muddy bike track, or skiing off piste--you need accurate, real-time information about your surroundings to pull off a successful trip. The X-Lander contributes by not only providing important data, but also keeping track of your activities so you can make rational decisions at key moments. In addition, the watch is user-friendly and solidly built, with a non-allergenic aluminum casing, a carbon-fiber back, a durable mineral crystal glass, and a water-resistant fabric strap.The built-in altimeter, which boasts a range of up to 29,500 feet, puts all 14 of the world's 8,000-plus-meter summits within the avid climber's range. Among the altimeter's functions are an altitude measurement function that lets you follow the vertical progress between stages, an automatic 24-hour memory that stores the altitude and ascent/decent rate for every hour, and an adjustable altitude alarm. Climbers will also dig the logbook function, which lets you record total and cumulative vertical ascents and descents as well as the number of runs skied.The X-Lander also displays the current barometric pressure and temperature--a must for activities in which weather plays a factor. The device automatically records barometric data for the previous four days, with the first six hours manifested in one-hour intervals and the rest in six-hour intervals. When the reference altitude is set correctly, the instrument also displays the present sea level pressure, which makes it easier to read and understand the barometric pressure at high altitudes.And few things are more important when exploring unfamiliar territory than a compass. The X-Lander's electronic compass contributes by guiding you with cardinal or half- cardinal points and a North-South arrow. The compass can also be set to track a certain bearing, which helps you follow a chosen direction. Meanwhile, the unit's declination adjustment function allows you to correct the difference between true North and magnetic North.In addition to the variety of outdoor functions, the X-Lander also displays normal time, with such add-ons as three daily alarms, a calendar programmed to the year 2089, a stopwatch with split-time measurement, and a countdown timer. Other features include a durable negative LCD display, a user-replaceable battery, and water-resistance to 100 feet. The X-Lander is backed by a two-year warranty on parts and labor.What's in the Box?X-Lander wrist-top computer, battery, user's manual.

reviewText: I purchased two of these watches after extensively reviewing the different types of pocket watches and customers' experience with them. I wanted a nice time piece with the option of putting a photograph of my father inside for myself and one with a photograph of me as a present for my father. I also remember being given a mechanical watch that was a prop from a high school play. That watch eventually fell to pieces, as I did not have the means to maintain it. The novelty of the watch remained, and I am pleased with its replacement almost 15 years later.The Charles Hubert 3846 is indeed a fine piece of craftsmanship despite being a modern watch. The two-tone accent is quite tasteful; even the bezel for the picture frame is not gaudy. As other reviews have mentioned, the watch does come with a silver chain which, in my opinion, looks better than a gold one since it allows the focus created by the watch's dual tone to remain on the watch; that being said, I am sure it would look fine with a gold chain and may try that option one day. I will add that I am very glad the watch came with a chain; I was promptly able to use it without having to wait to order one. I was a bit hesitant while looking at the size of the watch, but after purchasing it and examining it, I find that I thoroughly enjoy the heft and weight of the watch. Since I am an early riser and am in the habit of laying out my pocket items the night before, I rather enjoy winding this watch as part of my regimen. I would agree with the caution that one should wind the watch gingerly and stop winding when the crown no longer turns. For the technical eye, it is pleasant to see the machinations of the watch as it tells time and listen to it ticking. As for keeping time, the 3846 watch keeps pace with the quartz wristwatch I wear regularly. I must say that I am tempted to make the 3846 my regular time piece except that I live in Philadelphia; pulling a watch in and out of one's pocket is not the wisest way to tell time. If I continue to fancy doing so I may need to purchase a more subtle or plain time piece. That being said, those who have seen the watch say that it is beautiful, so I both concur and add to those who have gotten similar comments about their watch.I will offer a few cons to the pros, as nothing is perfect. To begin with, having instructions for removing the bezel and inserting and securing the photograph would have been useful. I assumed that there was a way to do it (i.e. it unscrewed or had clips) but doing so incorrectly could have resulted in unnecessary damage to the watch (e.g. stripping the bezel or losing the wire that holds the photograph). Secondly, since the watch goes the modern route of using glowing hands to enable time-keeping in the dark, it might have been useful to include glowing points where the numbers are-perhaps four marks at 12, 3, 6, and 9 to keep the subtlety of the watch. I can, however, appreciate the conservative nature of not including them and having a general idea of where the numbers are based on which way the hands are pointing. Thirdly, a brief schematic of the watch and some information about the watch (e.g. construction, location of features) would also have been useful, again for the purpose of either instructing the newcomer or reminding the novice. Finally, it would be nice if the crystal were glass instead of plastic, further adding to the watch's beauty and minimizing the possibility of scratches should the watch be in a pocket having other objects it it.Summarily, the Charles Hubert 3846 Two-Tone is a beautiful watch with pleasant design, observable time-keeping ability, and mechanical interest, which is why I rate it a 5-star watch. As an added bonus, I noticed that there was a silver version, and the magpie in me may consider adding that one to my collection. I am looking forward to presenting this watch to my father and wholeheartedly recommend it to any others looking at it for personal use or gift-giving.I. Dugan

reviewText: This watch may seem somewhat expensive since it is a black plastic basic time/date watch, but for what it is, it's perfect.  The plastic used to make the case is very high quality, the rubber used for the strap is very durable, but at the same time is comfortable/flexible/soft.  The many holes in the strap help keep your wrist from getting too sweaty, the numbers are big and easy to read, the accuracy of the watch is very impressive (loses maybe a minute or two per year), it's lightweight and it has a mineral crystal cover.  As an added bonus, the watch is not overly big/bulky...I have pretty small wrists and this watch doesn't look out of place when I wear it (note...the reviewer who posted his pics has REALLY tiny wrists...this is definitely not a big watch).  Also, this thing looks surprisingly classy for a plastic watch...I'm not saying you should wear it if you end up on the cover of Forbes mind you, but it really does look nice.I've had this watch for about 3 years now (haven't had to replace battery yet) and have been completely satisfied with it. If you are looking to purchase a simple but reliable/high-quality watch that can be worn anywhere,  this is probably the best one you can buy.

I ended up removing the loops on both the beads and watch and retying the entire thing (not before the beads came off three times-I could have saved some money and started from scratch!) but it was beautiful in the end.I would recommend for use without lobster clasps.

reviewText: This watch is not for everyone.  If you're looking to be like Dick Tracy, then look somewhere else.  I was looking for a watch that would let me get discreet notifications without having to pull out my phone every time.  It lets me triage what I have to answer and what can wait.  Battery life is great.  I'm getting about 4-5 days per charge.  It's a really light watch so it feels more like a silicone bracelet than a watch.I don't look at my phone nearly as often.  My kids are old enough to notice how often I look at my phone and know when I'm not paying attention to them.  When I'm not on call, I just place my phone on the counter and play with the kids.  Any notifications are triaged quickly and most of the time, I don't have to touch my phone.Changing watch faces is really easy - just press one button.  There are a couple of good apps that offer hundreds of different watch faces that you can download for free.  Downloading is really easy.  Change watch faces to fit your mood.I found that controlling my music from the watch is more convenient than I could have imagined.  Forward, back, and pause.  Anything else would be more easily done on your phone.  While driving, I just press a button without having to take my eyes off the road to go to the next song.Some reviewers have complained about the watch kicking off other bluetooth devices.  I did not find that to be the case.  My iphone 5 had no problem staying connected with both the Pebble and the car's bluetooth.A couple of minor complaints.  The resolution is the watch's weakest feature, but I will sacrifice some resolution for the long battery life.  Sometimes when the sun is shining at an angle to the watch, the light refracts and distorts the display a bit.One of the more pleasant effects since having the watch is that I no longer have the phantom vibration feeling in my leg thinking that my phone just vibrated.  Well worth the price.  Future versions can only improve on what is a fantastic watch thus far.

reviewText: Over the years I've owned several generations of Timex Ironman watches, along with other competitor's sports watches. This is the best so far and it is a pleasure to see that Timex is constantly refining and improving the Ironman brand in small and very useful ways. Small but extremely useful improvements over the last Ironman watch I owned include:- The Flix feature. This is very useful at night when you only have one hand available. Just activate the night mode, flick your wrist and the watch face illuminates for a few seconds.- When you press the Indiglo button, the face stays lit for a few seconds instead of only as long as you hold the button. Subtle change but big help.- When you press the Set button in any mode, helpful flashing icons appear which let you know which of the five buttons does what function (e.g. "+" to advance a number.) This pretty much eliminates ever needing to refer to the instruction manual.- The wristband curves where it interfaces with the watch for a better fit around your wrist.- The plastic loop which secures the un-notched portion of the band to the other half of the band has a notch which fits into a special hole in the free end of the band. This keeps the loose portion of the band secure around your wrist so that it never snags.The continual evolution in features, rock solid reliability, and excellent value for price will keep me a loyal Ironman user in the future.

title: Suunto Core Black Military
description: Building on the success of the venerable Suunto Vector, the Suunto Core keeps you informed of conditions while you hike, bike, or camp, making it a terrific companion for outdoor enthusiasts of all stripes. What can the Suunto Core do for you? For starters, it can sense an approaching squall even when the sky looks clear. This intelligent Storm Alarm--one of several intelligent features designed to keep you safe and secure--is activated by a rapid drop in air pressure over a three-hour period. Once the Core senses the change, the Storm Alarm sounds and flashes, letting you know that something unpleasant is fast approaching. The built-in altimeter, meanwhile, displays your current elevation, shows how much you've climbed or descended, and records your entire session for later analysis. Accurate to within 30,000 feet, the altimeter is an extremely valuable tool for mountaineering, backcountry skiing, and wilderness travel. Add in such features as a barometer, a digital thermometer, a weather trend indicator, and a digital compass and you have a terrific wrist-top computer for almost all your outdoor needs. Additional features include several traditional watch functions, including dual times, a date display, and an alarm; predicted times for sunrise and sunset to help you maximize your daylight hours; an automatic Alti/Baro mode that senses movement or lack thereof and switches between the altimeter and barometer accordingly; a depth meter that provides accurate water depth readings to 30 feet; and the ability to function in English, German, French, and Spanish. The Suunto Core carries a two-year warranty.

reviewText: I love these boots - they make taking the dogs out in the rain a little bit more fun! The quality is fantastic. reviewText: I have yet to buy a bad set of trunks. Call me lucky I guess. Though to be fair I have not ordered the new style Everlast Trunks, but Title, Ringside, a wide assortment of trunks from the stock, to custom, to heavy professional model. I love these for my workouts as an alternative to Basketball shorts from And 1, and Adidas I usually wear.There is a luxury feel from the Satin Poly fabic that is nice against you. For me at least.Length for me is about slightly above the knee. With the cut outs on the legs for better freedom of movement, thank you. Other details like the contrasting waistband, and the piping along the side looks great, and gives some style on what would be just another plain trunk. I would not say these are any better than the competition, and, they are certainly not worse. I think you could do better with your money with the Title Stock trunks, and pocket the change. Quality is about the same. With Everlast stock trunks, new style costing the same, yeah the ones I have no data points on is real close price wise too.Fit rating very good, construct, very good, seams, and details, very good. Value, just good.Contrast that with Title stock trunks, all the same, but value, excellent.Contrast with Title Pro trunks, and it goes from above, excellent, excellent, excellent, excellent.So in the end, though I like these, emotional choice part here, because of the style, and the Cleto Reyes name. Rational gear in place now, it is not the best value in the above metrics because Title, Ringside, and Everlast, supposition there, can do just as well for your money. Same smooth satiny feel, lightweight, fits well with your cup or protector if you box, so these rationally get a just recommended with the provision you emotionally decide Cleto Reyes is a must have. Otherwise you do have equal, if not better choices for your money. Thanks for reading.

reviewText: I expected a lot more from a "wrist computer" selling for almost 250.00, and the Military version for $300. First of all the visibility of the display is much too dark.  The images of the X-Lander on the Amazon and Suunto websites have been enhanced to the point that a case could be made for false advertising.  Secondly, the instructions to set the numeric values (meters vs feet, etc.) aren't even covered in the instructions that come with the watch, you have to download the full set of instructions to figure that out, then some of the fields used to set the values are so small and located in such bizarre locations, that even with 20/20 vision, I had to use an illuminated magnifying glass to see, then set the values.  Thirdly, the backlight feature is useless in low light or bright daylight.  It is only good for pitch black darkness...much too dim, but is probably the same as their military version, which has to be at a low level to keep the wearer from getting shot!  Fourth, (probably for the same reason) the alarm is not loud enough, especially if you are wearing the X-Lander under a couple of layers of clothing.  As others have stated, it should not be counted upon as a means to wake you from sleep.  Fifth, the barometric trend indicator is totally unreadable...too small and too dim to see under normal circumstances unless you also happen to be carrying a small foldout magnifying glass (which, as it turns out, I do carry while trekking).  Finally, the feature navigation is not intuitive, meaning if you do not use the features and sub-features regularly, good luck with remembering how some of the functions are accessed, and turned on and off, unless you carry the instructions on your person.I am going to keep this "wrist computer" for trekking, but it will not be the watch on my wrist for everyday casual use.  That honor will still go to my Wenger Military.  Because of that, there should be a way to shut off the X-Lander (short of removing the battery) so the battery does not run down while it's in the safe...still hoping to find out how to do that...doesn't have a stem to pull out like a watch.I can not recommend the X-Lander.  It is feature-rich, fairly compact and lightweight,  but the issues above make it less than desirable and overpriced.  The Finns need to address these issues before I buy another Suunto "wrist computer".
title: Suunto X-Lander Wrist-Top Computer Watch with Altimeter, Barometer, Compass, and Chronograph
description: The ultimate option for the outdoor enthusiast, the silver Suunto X-Lander wrist-top computer offers an accurate altimeter, a complete barometer, a precise electronic compass, and a multifunction sports watch in a single elegant package. Regardless of your excursion--whether it's climbing mountains, riding a muddy bike track, or skiing off piste--you need accurate, real-time information about your surroundings to pull off a successful trip. The X-Lander contributes by not only providing important data, but also keeping track of your activities so you can make rational decisions at key moments. In addition, the watch is user-friendly and solidly built, with a non-allergenic aluminum casing, a carbon-fiber back, a durable mineral crystal glass, and a water-resistant fabric strap.The built-in altimeter, which boasts a range of up to 29,500 feet, puts all 14 of the world's 8,000-plus-meter summits within the avid climber's range. Among the altimeter's functions are an altitude measurement function that lets you follow the vertical progress between stages, an automatic 24-hour memory that stores the altitude and ascent/decent rate for every hour, and an adjustable altitude alarm. Climbers will also dig the logbook function, which lets you record total and cumulative vertical ascents and descents as well as the number of runs skied.The X-Lander also displays the current barometric pressure and temperature--a must for activities in which weather plays a factor. The device automatically records barometric data for the previous four days, with the first six hours manifested in one-hour intervals and the rest in six-hour intervals. When the reference altitude is set correctly, the instrument also displays the present sea level pressure, which makes it easier to read and understand the barometric pressure at high altitudes.And few things are more important when exploring unfamiliar territory than a compass. The X-Lander's electronic compass contributes by guiding you with cardinal or half- cardinal points and a North-South arrow. The compass can also be set to track a certain bearing, which helps you follow a chosen direction. Meanwhile, the unit's declination adjustment function allows you to correct the difference between true North and magnetic North.In addition to the variety of outdoor functions, the X-Lander also displays normal time, with such add-ons as three daily alarms, a calendar programmed to the year 2089, a stopwatch with split-time measurement, and a countdown timer. Other features include a durable negative LCD display, a user-replaceable battery, and water-resistance to 100 feet. The X-Lander is backed by a two-year warranty on parts and labor.What's in the Box?X-Lander wrist-top computer, battery, user's manual.

title: Suunto X-Lander Wrist-Top Computer Watch with Altimeter, Barometer, Compass, and Chronograph
description: The ultimate option for the outdoor enthusiast, the silver Suunto X-Lander wrist-top computer offers an accurate altimeter, a complete barometer, a precise electronic compass, and a multifunction sports watch in a single elegant package. Regardless of your excursion--whether it's climbing mountains, riding a muddy bike track, or skiing off piste--you need accurate, real-time information about your surroundings to pull off a successful trip. The X-Lander contributes by not only providing important data, but also keeping track of your activities so you can make rational decisions at key moments. In addition, the watch is user-friendly and solidly built, with a non-allergenic aluminum casing, a carbon-fiber back, a durable mineral crystal glass, and a water-resistant fabric strap.The built-in altimeter, which boasts a range of up to 29,500 feet, puts all 14 of the world's 8,000-plus-meter summits within the avid climber's range. Among the altimeter's functions are an altitude measurement function that lets you follow the vertical progress between stages, an automatic 24-hour memory that stores the altitude and ascent/decent rate for every hour, and an adjustable altitude alarm. Climbers will also dig the logbook function, which lets you record total and cumulative vertical ascents and descents as well as the number of runs skied.The X-Lander also displays the current barometric pressure and temperature--a must for activities in which weather plays a factor. The device automatically records barometric data for the previous four days, with the first six hours manifested in one-hour intervals and the rest in six-hour intervals. When the reference altitude is set correctly, the instrument also displays the present sea level pressure, which makes it easier to read and understand the barometric pressure at high altitudes.And few things are more important when exploring unfamiliar territory than a compass. The X-Lander's electronic compass contributes by guiding you with cardinal or half- cardinal points and a North-South arrow. The compass can also be set to track a certain bearing, which helps you follow a chosen direction. Meanwhile, the unit's declination adjustment function allows you to correct the difference between true North and magnetic North.In addition to the variety of outdoor functions, the X-Lander also displays normal time, with such add-ons as three daily alarms, a calendar programmed to the year 2089, a stopwatch with split-time measurement, and a countdown timer. Other features include a durable negative LCD display, a user-replaceable battery, and water-resistance to 100 feet. The X-Lander is backed by a two-year warranty on parts and labor.What's in the Box?X-Lander wrist-top computer, battery, user's manual.
